# Sternenschweif – rekonstruierter Quelltext

## 225 Fehler behoben – 32 Jahre nach Release

**Inoffizielle Bugfix-Fassung · spielbar ohne Compiler · das Original bleibt unangetastet · [gleich loslegen](#schnellstart-bugfix-fassung-spielen-ohne-compiler)**

> **Zum ersten Mal seit 1994:** Nach der Gefangennahme durch die Orks liegt eure Ausrüstung wirklich in den Truhen,
> statt für immer zu verschwinden. Das Lagerhaus frisst euer Vermögen nicht mehr, Händler kassieren nur noch, was
> sie auch liefern, der Horriphobus-Kampf endet, und zwei Gespräche geben endlich den großen AP-Bonus, den Attic
> vorgesehen hatte. → [alle 225 Änderungen](BUGFIXES.md)

**Zusammen mit der [Schicksalsklinge](https://github.com/MeowMuhMuhCow/schicksalsklinge): 473 Bugfixes für DSA 1 und DSA 2.**

**Das Schwarze Auge 2: Sternenschweif** (Attic, 1994), deutsche CD-Fassung C1.02, vollständig als C/C++-Quelltext
rekonstruiert. Borland C++ 3.1 baut daraus eine `SCHWEIF.EXE`, die **Byte für Byte dem Original gleicht**
(MD5 `da3b59ce86a82e4b8bb14d36ed37d4d0`).

> **Passt zur GOG-Fassung:** Grundlage ist die deutsche `SCHWEIF.EXE` (CD-Version C1.02), wie sie in **„Realms of Arkania 2 - Star Trail Classic“ bei GOG** enthalten ist (MD5 `da3b59ce86a82e4b8bb14d36ed37d4d0`). Andere Fassungen (Diskette, englisch, andere Patchstände) ergeben eine andere EXE. Vor dem Bauen die eigene EXE mit dieser Prüfsumme vergleichen.

*English: Complete source reconstruction of the 1994 DOS RPG "Realms of Arkania: Star Trail" (German CD version 1.02, as sold by GOG).
Rebuilds a byte-identical executable with the original Borland C++ 3.1 compiler. Includes an unofficial bug-fix build (200+ original bugs fixed,
savegame compatible) behind compile-time switches. Documentation is in German.*

| | |
|---|---|
| Code | 301 Module in C/C++ (rund 119.000 Zeilen), 16 Module in Attics eigenem Assembler, alle kommentiert |
| Namen | alle 3.215 Funktionen und 1.941 Datenobjekte benannt (unsere Namen, Attics sind nicht erhalten) |
| Daten | jedes Modul trägt seine Daten selbst, so wie bei Attic |
| Fehler im Original | 268 dokumentiert, 18 kritisch, 22 Exploits ([Fehlerliste](Analyse/Fehlerliste_Sternenschweif.pdf)) |
| Fehlerbehebung | per Schalter `FIX_BUGS` 1 (wichtig) / 2 (alles), `FIX_EXPLOITS`, jeder Fehler einzeln. Ohne Schalter bytegleich ([FIXES.md](Bauen/FIXES.md)) |

## Schnellstart: Bugfix-Fassung spielen, ohne Compiler

**Alle Änderungen als übersichtliche Liste: [BUGFIXES.md](BUGFIXES.md).** Das fertige Paket zum Herunterladen gibt es unter **Releases** (rechts).

Für alle, die nur spielen wollen. Nötig sind Windows und Sternenschweif von GOG, sonst nichts: kein Python, kein Compiler.

1. Rechts unter **Releases** das Paket `…_Bugfix_1.0.zip` herunterladen (oder oben **Code → Download ZIP**) und irgendwohin entpacken.
2. **`PATCHEN.bat`** doppelklicken. Es findet den GOG-Spielordner (oder fragt danach), prüft per Prüfsumme, ob die
   eigene EXE genau die passende ist, und erzeugt daraus `Build\SCHWEIF_FIX_WICHTIG.EXE` und `Build\SCHWEIF_FIX_ALLES.EXE`.
   **Die Original-EXE wird nicht verändert**, das Spiel bleibt wie es ist.
3. **`SCHWEIF_FIX_WICHTIG_STARTEN.bat`** (wichtige Fehler) oder **`SCHWEIF_FIX_ALLES_STARTEN.bat`** (alle) doppelklicken.
   Das Spiel startet mit den GOG-Daten. Die Spielstände landen in eigenen Ordnern unter `Build\`, die echten bleiben unberührt.

**Funktionieren meine Spielstände weiter?** Ja. Die Bugfix-Fassung ändert das Speicherformat nicht, kein Feld, keine
Größe. Eure alten Spielstände aus dem GOG-Ordner erscheinen beim Laden automatisch und lassen sich weiterspielen.
Was ihr mit der Bugfix-Fassung neu speichert, landet in einem eigenen Ordner unter `Build\`. Eure Original-Spielstände
werden dabei nie überschrieben. Und weil das Format gleich bleibt, kann man jederzeit zurück zum Original. Speichern und Laden sind im Spiel getestet.

Der Patch (`Patch\*.ndp`, je 35–60 KB) enthält nur die geänderten Bytes, kein Originalprogramm. Ohne gekauftes
Spiel lässt sich damit nichts anfangen.

## Danke

Dieses Projekt (und schon sein Vorgehen) steht auf den Schultern von Menschen, die sich jahrelang, unbezahlt und aus reiner Liebe zu diesen
Spielen durch Maschinencode gearbeitet haben. **Ohne sie gäbe es das hier nicht.**

| | |
|---|---|
| **Henne** | Er hat im Projekt **Bright-Eyes** die Pionierarbeit für die Nordlandtrilogie geleistet: Die Schicksalsklinge Funktion für Funktion aus dem Maschinencode in binäräquivalenten Code zurückgewonnen, dazu die Werkzeuge und den Weg, den historischen Borland-Compiler in DOSBox anzusteuern. Über viele Jahre, größtenteils allein, mit einem Stundenaufwand, der sich kaum ermessen lässt. Er hat den Rohdiamanten ausgegraben. |
| **siebenstreich** | hat Bright-Eyes weitergeführt, den C-Code geschliffen und das Projekt am Leben gehalten (github.com/siebenstreich/BrightEyes), und hat unsere Fragen geduldig und offen beantwortet. |
| **cmfrydos** | entschlüsselt mit dem **Riva HD Viewer** die Datenformate der Nordlandtrilogie (Dungeons, Ereigniszonen, Dialoge, Kampfsystem) und teilt seine Ergebnisse offen im Forum und im Wiki. |
| **Das Crystals-DSA-Forum** | Seit 2006 sammeln die Spielerinnen und Spieler dort Fehler, Beobachtungen und Rätsel der Nordlandtrilogie, im Thread „Bugs in Sternenschweif“, in den Truhenpatch-Threads, in Tipps-Sammlungen und in der Technischen Werkstatt. Viele Einträge unserer Fehlerlisten gehen auf ihre Meldungen zurück und sind dort zuerst beschrieben worden. Danke an alle, die dort über die Jahre geschrieben, gemessen und nachgespielt haben, und an die Forenbetreiber, die das alles erhalten. |
| **Alle Beteiligten an Bright-Eyes, am BrightEyes-Wiki und an den Reverse-Engineering-Projekten der Nordlandtrilogie** | für Karten, Datenformate, Dokumentation und den langen Atem. |
| **Attic Entertainment Software** | für diese Spiele. 30 Jahre später lohnt es sich immer noch, jeden Winkel davon zu verstehen. |

Fehler in diesem Repository sind unsere eigenen. Alles, was gut daran ist, beruht auf ihrer Vorarbeit.

## Bugfix-Fassung: Sternenschweif ohne die Fehler von 1994

Neben dem originalgetreuen Bau gibt es eine **inoffizielle Fehlerbehebung**: über 200 Fehler aus dem Original
lassen sich per Schalter beheben, von Abstürzen über verlorene Ausrüstung bis zu falschen Händlerpreisen.

| | |
|---|---|
| Stufe „wichtig“ | kritische und mittlere Fehler (u. a. Lagerhaus mit explodierendem Warenwert, Orks werfen Ausrüstung weg, Ware bezahlt aber nicht erhalten, Kräuterwirkungen verfallen nicht, Horriphobus-Kampf endet nie, Absturz am Schlüsselbund) |
| Stufe „alles“ | zusätzlich viele kleine Fehler ohne große Spielwirkung |
| Exploits | standardmäßig mit behoben (z. B. Geld aus der Spende, endlose Truhe). Wer sie behalten will: `FIX_EXPLOITS 0` |
| Spielstände | **kompatibel**, das Speicherformat ist unverändert. Alte Spielstände lassen sich weiterspielen |
| Bauen | `Bauen\BAUEN.bat wichtig` oder `Bauen\BAUEN.bat alles` → `Build\SCHWEIF_FIX_WICHTIG.EXE` bzw. `SCHWEIF_FIX_ALLES.EXE` |
| Spielen | `SCHWEIF_FIX_WICHTIG_STARTEN.bat` bzw. `SCHWEIF_FIX_ALLES_STARTEN.bat` (eigene Spielstand-Ordner) |
| Stand | statisch vollständig geprüft, im Spiel angetestet (Start, Herberge, Speichern/Laden). **Tester willkommen** – Prüfliste in [Analyse/Bericht_Fehler_Patches.md](Analyse/Bericht_Fehler_Patches.md) |

Welcher Fehler wie behoben ist und was bewusst nicht geändert wurde (Spielstandformat, Absicht unklar): [Bauen/FIXES.md](Bauen/FIXES.md).
Alle Fehler verständlich beschrieben, mit Cheat-Liste: [Fehlerliste](Analyse/Fehlerliste_Sternenschweif.pdf).

## Bauen (Windows)

Kurzfassung, ausführlich in [START_HIER.md](START_HIER.md):

1. Python 3 installieren.
2. Borland C++ 3.1 besorgen (z. B. https://archive.org/details/bcpp31) und nach `Compiler\` kopieren (`BIN`, `INCLUDE`, `LIB`).
3. Die eigene `SCHWEIF.EXE` aus der GOG-Installation nach `Original\` kopieren (nur zum Vergleich).
4. `Bauen\BAUEN.bat` starten → „BYTEGLEICH mit dem Original“. Mit `BAUEN.bat wichtig` bzw. `alles` zusätzlich die Fassung mit Fehlerbehebungen.
5. `SCHWEIF_STARTEN.bat` bzw. `SCHWEIF_FIX_WICHTIG_STARTEN.bat` startet das Spiel mit den GOG-Daten.

## Aufbau

| Ordner | Inhalt |
|---|---|
| `Quelle/` | der Quelltext: residente Module, `Overlays/`, Header in `inc/` (`schweif.h`) |
| `Bauen/` | Bau-Paket für Windows (`BAUEN.bat`, `bauen.py`) |
| `Analyse/` | Fehlerliste, Quelltextkarte (`Quelltextkarte.html`), Berichte (3D-Engine, Audio, Kopierschutz, Datensegment) |
| `Werkzeuge/` | die Werkzeuge der Rekonstruktion |

Lesereihenfolge und Begriffe: [LIESMICH.md](LIESMICH.md). Gesamtbericht: [ABSCHLUSSBERICHT.md](ABSCHLUSSBERICHT.md).

## Wie es gemacht wurde

Das Originalprogramm wurde in Module zerlegt und als Assembler wieder bytegleich zusammengebaut. Danach wurde jede
Funktion in C/C++ neu geschrieben und mit dem Original-Compiler gegen den Assembler geprüft, bis das Ergebnis
übereinstimmte. Der Compiler ist dabei der Schiedsrichter: gleich oder nicht gleich.

## Rechte

Kein Originalprogramm, keine Spieldaten, kein Compiler in diesem Repository. Rechte am Spiel bei den Rechteinhabern.
Details: [RECHTE.md](RECHTE.md).

MooMoo mit Claude, Oktober 2026.

batenkaitos-dev-mh2-decomp-readme-md.text:
# Monster Hunter 2 (Dos) decompilation

A research and preservation project: a matching decompilation of
**Monster Hunter 2 (Dos)** for the PlayStation 2 (NTSC-J, version 1.04,
`SLPM_662.80`; Capcom, 2006).

- **Capcom's code is decompiled and matches.** All 12,532 of its functions
  are built from this repository's source to the original's exact bytes:
  12,520 as C, compiled by the game's original compiler, and 12 as
  Capcom's own hand-written assembly. The build reproduces the boot
  executable and all 12 code overlays byte for byte.
- **The libraries Capcom licensed are not decompiled:** Sony's SDK, CRI's
  middleware, the network libraries and ACCESS's kana-kanji engine. The
  build takes them from your copy of the game.
- **DNAS, and the values of the game's data and texts, come from your
  copy** at build time.

The table under [Status](#status) gives the bytes of each.

The code matches, and it has had a full readability pass. That work was
deliberately left until the whole build matched, so that every cleanup
could be checked against it: the functions, data and fields are named and
typed, each C file has its header, and the data's tables have their own
types. Corrections and further cleanup are welcome (see
[Contributing](#contributing)).

The project exists to preserve how the game works, in a form people can
read, and to show how a large PS2 title was made: how a 2006 CodeWarrior
codebase of over 12,500 functions was written, compiled and laid out.

**This repository contains no game data.** It holds the code and the
structure of the game's data (types, names, sizes). Everything else comes
from your own copy of the game when you build.

## Status

Where each byte of the 13 built files comes from (`ninja provenance`, from
the link maps):

| Origin | Bytes | Share | From your copy? |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| Capcom's code, compiled from C | 4,633,096 | 53.7% | no |
| zlib 1.1.4 (third-party), compiled from its decompiled C | 20,032 | 0.2% | no |
| Data the compiler makes from the C: tables written in C, literals, jump tables | 203,980 | 2.4% | no |
| Assembly from the repository's source: main's copy loops, the VU1 microcode | 107,568 | 1.2% | no |
| Capcom's data, described in C, with its values from your copy | 1,654,752 | 19.2% | by policy: the game's content |
| Third-party libraries, code and data | 1,134,560 | 13.2% | yes: not decompiled |
| DNAS: its two overlays and its authentication data | 862,352 | 10.0% | yes |
| Headers and zero padding | 3,868 | 0.0% | no: the link could write them |
| **Placed by the link** (`.bss` aside) | **8,620,208** | 100% | |

The first four rows, 4,964,676 bytes (57.6%), are built from the
repository's source. The rest of each file is the linker's alignment fill.

- **Complete.** All 12,532 of Capcom's functions are source and match (the
  `game` row of `ninja progress`); no `NON_MATCHING` block is left.
  - 12,478 are C.
  - 42 are CodeWarrior `asm` functions in their C files
    (`src/sub_main/engine_math.c`, `anim_curve.c` and `vu1_packets.c`): VU0
    code, which MWCC never emits from C
    ([docs/mwcc-matching.md](docs/mwcc-matching.md), "What can't come from
    C").
  - 12 are main's hand-written copy and fill loops
    ([src/main/mem_loops.s](src/main/mem_loops.s)), which no C produces.
  - The VU1 microcode (60 programs) is VU1 assembly
    ([src/sub_main/vu1_microcode.vsm](src/sub_main/vu1_microcode.vsm)),
    built by the project's own assembler, `tools/vu1as.py`.
    `config/overlays/sub_main.yaml` lists the block as `textbin`: that is
    splat's copy from your disc, which objdiff compares against; the build
    assembles the source in its place.
- **zlib 1.1.4**, which the lobby links (inflate and adler32), is
  decompiled too and counted apart (the `zlib` row): its 19 functions
  match, in `src/lobby/adler32.c`, `infblock.c`, `inflate.c` and
  `infutil.c`.
- **Byte for byte.** The build reproduces the boot executable and all 12
  overlays; `ninja` checks all 13 against
  [config/targets.sha1](config/targets.sha1). Four of the overlays hold no
  Capcom code: `dnas_net` and `dnas_ins` (Sony's DNAS2 library, copied from
  your disc as is), `lbguild` (data only) and `test` (a 256-byte all-zero
  stub).
- **Checked by every build.** `ninja` also compiles each C file a second
  time with plain MWCC, with none of the build's wrapper, and compares
  every function with the build's (`tools/plain_check.py`: 12,539 of 12,539
  identical, Capcom's and zlib's), and fails if any code comes from
  anything but `src/`, the repository's assembly or a labelled library
  piece (`tools/provenance.py --check`).
- **Counted apart.** Code that Capcom licensed rather than wrote has rows
  of its own in `ninja progress` and is not decompiled: Sony's EE libraries
  (with the toolchain's C library, libm, libgcc and CodeWarrior's runtime),
  CRI's middleware, the network libraries (nethttp's HTTPS and
  OpenSSL-derived code, and DNAS) and ACCESS's kana-kanji engine in
  sub_main. The build takes it from your copy: splat turns it into
  assembly, except DNAS, whose bytes are copied as they are. Its names are
  in [config/symbols/](config/symbols/). Over the whole program, 12,552 of
  17,326 functions (75.6% of 6.19 MB of code) are source: Capcom's 12,532,
  zlib's 19, and the VU1 microcode, which `ninja progress` counts as one.
- **Data and text** are described in C, not stored in it: each object's
  type, name and size are in the source, and its values and the game's
  texts come from your copy at build time
  ([CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md), "Content"). The one object kept as
  a copy of its bytes is DNAS's authentication data (64 KB in sub_main, an
  `INCLUDE_DATA` line in `src/sub_main/dnas_check.c`).
- **Readability.** All 12,551 functions, Capcom's and zlib's, have real
  names (the `named` column of `ninja progress`). What is left to name and
  tidy (fields and data objects) is under [Contributing](#contributing).

## Your copy of the game

The build reads your own copy of the disc: either the `.iso` or the
extracted disc files. Only version 1.04 is supported; other releases and
reprints may have different executables.

By default, the tools look for your files in the **parent directory of the
repository**: the disc files directly there (`SYSTEM.CNF`,
`SLPM_662.80`, ...), or the `.iso` there or one folder below. To use
another place, set `MH2_ORIG_DIR`:

```sh
export MH2_ORIG_DIR=/path/to/mh2
```

The tools treat your files as read-only: they never modify, move or delete
them. `python tools/verify_originals.py` checks your copy against the
known-good hashes of version 1.04 (the Redump dump) in
[config/disc.sha1](config/disc.sha1).

`asm/`, `assets/` and everything under `build/` (including `build/gen/`,
the data values and texts) are generated from your copy and gitignored.
They are for your own use: don't share them.

## Building

The matching build runs on **Linux** x86-64 (tested on Ubuntu 24.04); on
Windows, it runs inside **WSL 2**. Everything is installed into the
repository's `tools/deps/` (gitignored) at pinned versions:
[tools/versions.txt](tools/versions.txt), whose downloads are checked
against their SHA-256, and [uv.lock](uv.lock) for Python. That takes about
400 MB, and a build about 210 MB more.

### Linux

You need `git`, and `sudo` on Debian or Ubuntu, where the setup script
installs `ca-certificates`, `curl`, `git`, `tar` and `clang` with apt
(clang reads the C files' types for `tools/content_gen.py`). On another
distribution, install those yourself and run `tools/setup.sh --no-apt`.

```sh
git clone <repository URL> mh2-decomp
cd mh2-decomp
tools/setup.sh                   # once: the pinned toolchain, into tools/deps/
source tools/env.sh              # in every new shell
export MH2_ORIG_DIR=/path/to/mh2 # unless your copy is in the parent directory
python tools/verify_originals.py # optional: check your copy
python tools/configure.py        # extract the targets from your copy, split them, write build.ninja
ninja                            # generate the content, compile, assemble, link, check the 13 targets
ninja progress                   # matched code per module and by origin
ninja provenance                 # where each byte of the 13 files comes from
```

`ninja` ends with one line per target:

```
OK    SLPM_662.80
OK    select.bin
...
OK    sub_main.bin
```

**`OK` for all 13** means that each built file's SHA-1 equals the game's
([config/targets.sha1](config/targets.sha1)): your build is
byte-identical to the original. The first `configure.py` takes about a
minute and a half, and a full build a little over a minute with 8 jobs.

The setup script keeps its downloads in `tools/deps/downloads/` and
fetches only what is missing there, so a second checkout can reuse a first
one's: `mkdir -p tools/deps && ln -s /path/to/first/tools/deps/downloads
tools/deps/downloads` before `tools/setup.sh`.

### Windows

1. Install WSL 2 with Ubuntu 24.04 (Microsoft's WSL documentation
   describes how), then open an Ubuntu shell.
2. In Ubuntu, clone the repository into the Linux file system (for
   example `~/mh2-decomp`): the build is much faster there than under
   `/mnt/c`.
3. Follow the Linux steps. Your disc files can stay on Windows: for a copy
   in `D:\games\mh2`, `export MH2_ORIG_DIR=/mnt/d/games/mh2`.

The game's compiler is a Windows program; wibo runs it on Linux, and
there is no native Windows build.

### A readable copy, for your own use

After `configure.py`, `python tools/export_readable.py` writes
`build/readable/`, a copy of the source with your copy's data tables and
texts written out in C (each struct member by its field name). It builds
the same way, byte-identical until you edit it. It holds the game's
content: keep it on your machine, and never commit or share it
([CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md), "The readable export").

## Project layout

| Path | What it is |
|---|---|
| `src/<module>/` | Capcom's code: C, one file per translation unit; main's hand-written assembly; sub_main's VU1 microcode |
| `include/` | headers: `common.h`, one for each C file (or its subject), one for each library's functions, and the `*.spec` files some structs are generated from |
| `config/` | splat configs (`main.yaml`, `overlays/<module>.yaml`), names (`symbols/`), function starts (`functions/`), linker aliases (`ld/`), described assets (`assets/`), the reviewed exceptions of the content check (`content_exceptions.txt`), the known-good hashes (`disc.sha1`, `targets.sha1`) |
| `tools/` | setup, build, verification and diffing scripts ([tools/README.md](tools/README.md)) |
| `docs/` | the MWCC matching reference ([docs/mwcc-matching.md](docs/mwcc-matching.md)), notes on hard matches (`docs/notes/hard-matches/`), how the project was made ([docs/ai-workflow/](docs/ai-workflow/README.md)) |
| `asm/`, `assets/`, `build/` | generated from your copy (gitignored) |

`main` is the boot executable, `SLPM_662.80`; the other modules are the
code overlays stored in the disc's `DATA.BIN`.

## How it matches

- **The compiler** is Metrowerks CodeWarrior for PS2, compiler build
  `3.0b52-030722`, with the flags `-O3,p -sdatathreshold 0 -str readonly`
  (and `#pragma optimization_level` where the game built a file or a
  function at another level). It was chosen by compiling candidates and
  comparing their output with the game's code. The setup script downloads
  it from decomp.me's compiler archive, and the build runs it through
  wibo.
- **splat** splits the boot executable and the overlays by the YAML files
  in `config/`, with spimdisasm and rabbitizer disassembling the R5900
  code. That is where the libraries' assembly comes from.
- **`tools/content_gen.py`** writes the data values and texts the C
  includes, from your copy, with the types clang reads from the C.
- **`tools/mwcc_cc.py`** compiles each C file, converted from UTF-8 to
  Shift-JIS (the game's encoding). It changes how MWCC's output is laid
  out, never its code: it removes its own marker variables, makes static
  functions' symbols global, keeps every data object in a section of its
  own with its alignment raised to at least 8 (the game's), moves the
  variables between `#pragma rodata on` and `off` to `.rodata`, splices in
  the one copied object (`INCLUDE_DATA`), and drops the `Stripped_`
  functions, stand-ins for code the game's linker removed.
  `tools/plain_check.py` shows that no code byte changes. binutils, built
  for the PS2's R5900, assembles and links, and `tools/check_targets.py`
  compares the results with the game's hashes.
- **The boot executable's `.comment`** reads `MW MIPS C Compiler
  (2.4.1.01)`. That label comes from CodeWarrior's linker: the string is in
  the `mwldps2.exe` that comes with the compiler, whose own `mwccps2.exe`
  says 3.0.0. It doesn't point to another compiler.
- **objdiff** diffs each unit against the original, function by function,
  and makes the progress report; `tools/func_diff.py` checks one file's
  functions in about a second.
- [docs/mwcc-matching.md](docs/mwcc-matching.md) is the project's
  reference on which C gives which instructions with this compiler: its
  register allocator, its scheduler, and a catalogue of patterns.

The project stands on these tools:

| Tool | By | Used for |
|---|---|---|
| [splat](https://github.com/ethteck/splat) | ethteck | splitting the executables |
| [spimdisasm](https://github.com/Decompollaborate/spimdisasm), [rabbitizer](https://github.com/Decompollaborate/rabbitizer) | Decompollaborate | disassembly |
| [binutils-mips-ps2-decompals](https://github.com/decompals/binutils-mips-ps2-decompals) | decompals | assembling and linking for the R5900 |
| [wibo](https://github.com/decompals/wibo) | decompals | running the Windows compiler on Linux |
| [decomp.me's compiler archive](https://github.com/decompme/compilers) | decompme | the MWCC download |
| [objdiff](https://github.com/encounter/objdiff) | encounter | diffs and progress reports |
| [decomp-permuter](https://github.com/simonlindholm/decomp-permuter) | simonlindholm | finding C variants that match (settings in `tools/`) |
| [m2c](https://github.com/matt-kempster/m2c) | matt-kempster | the first drafts of the C |
| [uv](https://github.com/astral-sh/uv) | astral-sh | the pinned Python environment |
| [ninja](https://github.com/ninja-build/ninja) | ninja-build | running the build |
| [clang](https://github.com/llvm/llvm-project) | llvm | reading the C's types for the content generator |
| [pyelftools](https://github.com/eliben/pyelftools), [pycdlib](https://github.com/clalancette/pycdlib) | eliben; clalancette | reading ELF files and the disc image |

## Contributing

The code matches; what's open is making it read well, and anyone can
help:
- name the `unk` fields in `include/` (and those in structs local to one
  file) and the data objects still named by address;
- give the small groups of raw byte-offset accesses their struct fields;
- replace a fakematch (`git grep FAKEMATCH`) with a natural form that
  matches.

Every change must keep `ninja` at `OK` for all 13 targets and
`tools/proto_check.py` at 0 disagreements, and add no game content
(`python tools/content_scan.py`: 0 findings).
[CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) has the checks, the conventions, the
tools and the counts of what is left.

## Made with AI

Claude, Anthropic's AI model (Claude Opus 5.5), did the work in Claude
Code; the project's owner, Batenkaitos, directed it and made the
decisions.

- **What the build guarantees:** the 13 files are byte-identical to the
  game's, every function of Capcom's and zlib's compiles to the original's
  exact bytes, and none of Capcom's code comes from your copy
  ([Status](#status)).
- **What it doesn't:** names, types, comments and explanations are the
  AI's reading of the code, and can be wrong. Corrections are welcome.

More in [docs/ai-workflow/](docs/ai-workflow/README.md).

## Legal

- This is an unofficial project, not affiliated with or endorsed by Capcom
  or Sony Interactive Entertainment. Monster Hunter is a trademark of
  Capcom Co., Ltd., and PlayStation is a trademark of Sony Interactive
  Entertainment Inc.; all trademarks belong to their owners.
- The repository contains no game data, executables, assets, text or SDK
  files. Building it requires your own legally obtained copy of the game.
- The game links zlib 1.1.4. Its code here, in `src/lobby/`
  (`adler32.c`, `infblock.c`, `inflate.c` and `infutil.c`) with its header
  `include/zlib.h`, keeps zlib's own licence notice.

# Civilization (1991, v475.01) — recompiled to C

This directory turns the original DOS `CIV.EXE` (plus its overlays and the
MGRAPHIC / sound drivers) into C source that builds natively for Linux
(SDL2) and for DOS (DJGPP).  The original game files are still needed at
run time (graphics, text, and the program image itself).

**The generated source is derived from your copy of the game. Keep it
private; do not redistribute it.**

## Running

    make                 # builds ./civ (needs gcc, SDL2, zlib)
    ./civ                # reads civ.cfg: 1920x1080, widescreen, fullscreen

Useful options (all also valid in `civ.cfg` as `name = value`):

| option | meaning |
|---|---|
| `--res 1920x1080` | window / screen size |
| `--fullscreen` | fullscreen (Alt+Enter toggles) |
| `--widescreen` | wider map view filling the screen (square pixels) |
| `--classic` | original 320x200, letterboxed at 4:3 |
| `--zoom N` | widescreen: screen pixels per game pixel (default height/200) |
| `--mapwidth N` | world width in squares, even, 80 (original) to 160; height stays 50 |
| `--realtime` | turns pass on a clock (see below) |
| `--turnsecs S` | realtime: seconds per turn (default 3) |
| `--barbarians 0` | no barbarians: no raids, uprisings or barbarians from huts |
| `--rankings 0` | no historians' reports (wealthiest, largest ... civilizations); always off in multiplayer |
| `--sound none\|speaker` | sound driver (AdLib emulation is not implemented yet) |
| `--setup` | ask the original graphics / sound / mouse questions |
| `--gamedir DIR` | where the original files are |

Widescreen at 1920x1080 gives a 384x216 game screen at 5x: the map view is
19x13 squares instead of 15x12.  Other screens (city, reports, intro) keep
their 320x200 layout and are shown centred.

`make run` builds and starts the game.

## Added features

* **Produce gold** — in a city's "What shall we build" list (CHANGE on the
  city screen, or when production is due) pick **Gold: production to
  treasury**; picking anything else from the list switches it off again.
  The GOLD button (bottom right of the city screen, next to EXIT) and the
  **G** key toggle it too.  While it is on ("GOLD!") the city's production
  goes into your treasury each turn instead of the production box, so
  nothing gets built.  The setting is saved with the game (`CIVILn.NAT`
  next to `CIVILn.SVE`).
* **Auto-work settlers** — press **A** on an active Settlers unit.  It
  improves the 21 squares of the nearest own city (within 2 squares), or
  the 5x5 squares around it: road, then railroad, then irrigation (not on
  forest, swamp or jungle, where irrigating changes the terrain).  Orders
  the game refuses (no Railroad yet, no water nearby) are skipped and
  retried in a later pass once new work has been done.  Press any key while
  the settlers are active to take control back.

* **Mouse wheel zoom** (widescreen) — on the map, the wheel changes the
  size of a game pixel: at 1920x1080 5x (19x13 squares), 4x (25x16) or 3x
  (35x22).  The view never gets wider than half the world.
* **Drag-scroll** — drag the map with the left (or right) button; a click
  without moving still goes to the game as before.  Zoom and scrolling are
  applied while the game waits for your orders.

* **Real-time mode** (`realtime = 1`) — time passes even when you do
  nothing: each turn lasts a few seconds (default 3) and then ends by
  itself, the other civilizations move and the year advances.  Units with
  goto orders (**G**, then click the destination) walk on every turn, so
  fast units cover more ground than slow ones.  **Tab** switches to the next
  unit, **clicking** one of your units makes it the active one (cancelling
  its standing orders).  **[** / **-** slower, **]** / **=** faster, **F12**
  pause.  The bar at the bottom of the status panel shows the turn time.
  Dialogs, menus and city screens stop the clock.  A discovered advance
  is announced with a short message instead of the picture and dialog.
* **Multiplayer over the network** — two PCs on the same network play one
  game in real time.  Choose **Multiplayer** in the start menu: **H** hosts
  a game, **F** searches the network (UDP broadcast) and lists the games
  found; **Enter** joins.  When the other player is in, the host presses
  **Enter** and starts a new game as usual; the joining player gets one of
  the other civilizations.  Both play at the same time; the turn clock (the
  host's `turnsecs`) keeps running; nothing is closed for you: a turn that
  is due ends when you are back on the map (while the host has a city
  screen or dialog open, the host's game waits there).  Ports: TCP 28400, UDP 28401.  Both need the same
  `mapwidth`.

  How it works: the host's game is the real one.  At every turn start it
  sends the game state (the game's own save data plus the map) to the other
  PC, whose player plays on it at the same time.  The orders given there
  (unit moves and orders, goto targets, city builds, gold settings, tax
  and science rates, research goal) are
  sent to the host twice a second.  When the host's turn clock runs out,
  the units on both PCs are done; the other PC sends its last orders at
  once and the host carries them out in the same turn, so what was done
  there stays.  You stay on the map (or in your city screen) until the next
  state arrives (a player in a city screen or dialog is not waited for;
  their later orders count for the next turn).  Diplomacy of the joining
  player's civilization is still decided by the computer.
* **Wider worlds** — `--mapwidth 160` (or `mapwidth = 160` in `civ.cfg`)
  makes the world up to twice as wide; it still wraps east-west.  New
  random worlds use the whole width (land amount scales with it), AI
  civilizations start anywhere, and EARTH is stretched to the chosen width.
  The minimap shows an 80 column window that follows the view; the world
  map and the end-of-game replay show 80 columns around your capital.
  Saved games of a wider world need the same `--mapwidth` to load (the map
  layers are in `CIVILn.WMP` next to the save) and can't be loaded by the
  original game.

Code: `src/native/capital.c`, `src/native/autowork.c`, `src/native/mapnav.c`,
`src/native/mapsize.c` (wide map support), `src/native/realtime.c`,
`src/native/mp.c` and `mp_net.c` (multiplayer), overlay drawing in
`src/native/overlay.c`; the hook points are in `tools/hooks.txt`.

## DOS build

    make dos             # -> civ.exe (DPMI host embedded, no CWSDPMI.EXE needed)

Uses the DJGPP cross compiler in `toolchain/djgpp` (prebuilt GCC 12.2 from
github.com/andrewwutw/build-djgpp) and CWSDPMI from delorie.com, both
downloaded into `toolchain/`.  Copy `civ.exe` into the game directory under
another name (e.g. `CIVR.EXE`, the original `CIV.EXE` must stay) and run it.
The DOS build uses real VGA mode 13h and the classic 320x200 layout.

## Layout

    tools/        lifter (x86-16 -> C) and analysis / test tools (Python)
      lift.py       the static recompiler
      seeds.txt     extra code entry points (only reachable via pointers)
      patches.txt   instruction constants, segments and displacements replaced
                    by expressions (widescreen, wider maps)
      hooks.txt     native functions called before given instructions
      overrides.txt lifted functions replaced by hand written C
    src/gen/      generated C, one file per code segment / overlay / driver
    src/native/   hand written replacements of game functions
    runtime/      CPU helpers, DOS/BIOS/VGA/PIT/mouse emulation, native
                  graphics driver (gfx.c), SDL and DOS platform layers,
                  8086 interpreter (fallback + reference)
    tests/        differential test harnesses; tests/scripts: input scripts
                  for the run checks below

`make lift` regenerates `src/gen` from `../CIV` (Python 3 with capstone and
unicorn: `tools/py` points at a virtualenv; recreate it with
`python3 -m venv venv && venv/bin/pip install capstone unicorn` and edit
`tools/py`).

## How it works

* `CIV.EXE` is EXEPACK-compressed; the root image, 23 MS-LINK overlays and
  the drivers are disassembled by recursive descent (1258 functions).
* Each function becomes a C function operating on an emulated register file
  and 1 MB of real-mode memory, so behaviour is exactly the original's.
  Flag computations are only emitted where a later instruction reads them,
  and compare+branch pairs become plain C conditions.
* A shadow call stack handles the program's tricks: thunks that pop their
  own return address, `_setargv`/`__chkstk` stack games, self-modifying
  driver thunks (executed through the interpreter), INT 3Fh overlay calls.
* The runtime emulates DOS (files, memory blocks, EXEC 4B03 driver loading,
  FCBs), BIOS (video, keyboard, timer), PIC/PIT/keyboard controller, VGA DAC
  and an INT 33h mouse.
* The MCGA graphics driver is reimplemented natively (`runtime/gfx.c`) so
  screen pages can be any size; in classic mode it can be checked against
  the original driver call by call (`CIV_GFX=shadow`).

## Adding features

Replace a lifted function with C: add its name (e.g. `f_1b05_0004`) to
`tools/overrides.txt`, run `make lift`, and define the function in
`src/native/*.c`.  The original stays callable as `lifted_<name>`; see
`src/native/mapview.c` for an example (arguments via `FARG(n)`, game
variables via `GW()/GB()`, finish with `RET_FAR(0)`).  For single constants
use `tools/patches.txt`.

`tools/dumpfunc.py ../CIV root SEG:OFF` prints the disassembly of a function.

## Testing

    make test       # every distinct instruction vs unicorn (102k cases)
    make functest   # whole pure functions vs unicorn
    tools/compare_runs.sh tests/scripts/monkey1d.txt
                                   # lifted vs interpreter, deterministic trace
    tools/widestore_check.sh       # wide map storage at width 80 vs the original
                                   # layout: game state must be the same
    tools/mp_check.sh              # multiplayer: host + joining game on one PC
    HOSTCIV=3 tools/mp_check.sh    # same test, host plays civ 3
    CIV_GFX=shadow  # native graphics driver vs original, per call

Test runs use a copy of the game in `build/game` (they save games).
`CIV_ORIGINAL=1` leaves the game's menus unchanged (no Multiplayer and Gold
entries), as the comparison runs need.  `CIV_MPDEBUG=1` logs multiplayer
turns and orders.

Debug aids: `CIV_WATCHDOG=N`, `CIV_DUMP=secs`, `CIV_TRACE=file`
(`CIV_TRACE_STACK=1` adds the call stack, lifted runs only), `CIV_ITRACE=n`,
`CIV_MAPTRACE=file` (map square writes), `CIV_GFXDEBUG=1`, `--script FILE`
(see runtime/script.c).  Analysis helpers: `tools/mapscan.py`,
`tools/widthscan.py` (map width constants), `tools/ctxat.sh MOD SEG:OFF`.

## Known limitations

* Widescreen: dialogs over the map are still placed for 320x200 (left of
  centre); some view-size constants deeper in unit/city code may remain
  unpatched — report odd behaviour near the right/bottom of the map view.
* No AdLib/Sound Blaster emulation yet (PC speaker works); text-mode setup
  screen is printed to the terminal, not drawn in the window.
* A rare timing-dependent "divide error" was seen once at startup in
  widescreen and could not be reproduced; the message shows a call stack.
* The DOS build compiles and links but could not be run here (DOSBox needs
  a display); untested on real DOS.

# gp64

Run Geoff Crammond's original Formula One Grand Prix (F1GP) on Windows 11 and macOS.
Copy gp64 into your existing game folder and run it. The game starts as it
did on a DOS PC, with its own graphics, sound, controls and two-player links.

gp64 runs your own unmodified copy by emulation, not decompilation. Under the
hood it is a cut-down DOS emulator in Rust: a real-mode PC, DOS and BIOS
services, VGA video, keyboard and mouse, PC speaker and AdLib audio, and a
null-modem cable and a serial modem carried over TCP on the local network.
No DOS installation or ROM image is required.

This is a personal project with irregular maintenance. Contributions and pull
requests are not accepted; forks are welcome under GPL-3.0-or-later. There is no
promise of support, fixes or future releases. See [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md).

## Screenshots

Two copies of gp64 on one PC, linked by their emulated modems: one dials while
the other waits for the call.

![Two gp64 windows: one dialling, one waiting for the call](docs/screenshots/modem-link.png)

The race start, seen from both linked copies.

![Two gp64 windows on the starting grid](docs/screenshots/race-start.png)

A fastest-lap message arriving on both copies at once.

![Two gp64 windows showing the same fastest-lap message](docs/screenshots/fastest-lap.png)

There's a video here as well: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PeTzJTES8a8

## Drop-in launch

Copy gp64 into your own F1GP folder and run it. It starts the normal batch launcher, or the executable if the batch file is absent.

The folder is mounted as writable drive C:, so the program can save its own
settings and progress. An explicit program path mounts that program's folder
instead. Recording starts only when requested with `--record` or from the
F12 menu. Menu recordings go to the user's video folder, with a fallback when
that folder is unavailable.

```sh
./gp64
./gp64 --mute
./gp64 /path/to/program.exe argument
```

## Options and controls

```text
gp64 [--mute] [--record FILE] [--script FILE] [--wait] [program [args]]
```

- `--mute`: disable host audio output.
- `--record FILE`: record video and audio to an MKV/WebM file, finalised on exit.
- `--script FILE`: drive the program from an emuscru script, then exit (see
  [Scripted runs](#scripted-runs)). Implies `--wait`.
- `--wait`: on Windows, keep the prompt until gp64 exits and print its messages
  there. Without it, gp64 returns to the prompt once started and shows a
  failure in a message box.
- `--help` and `--version`: print help or version.

For two players, run gp64 on two machines on the same local network, or twice
on one machine. In each copy, turn on F12 → Serial for a null-modem cable on
COM1, or F12 → Modem for a modem on COM2. The two copies find each other and
connect by themselves; the menu row shows the other machine once connected.
Then use F1GP's own serial-link or modem setup on that COM port.

In F1GP's link setup, choose the fastest port speed, such as 19200. That
setting is the speed of the cable between the PC and its modem, not the
modem's line speed (gp64's modem connects at up to 14400). F1GP exchanges
data every frame, so on a 2400 bps cable it spends most of its time waiting
and plays slowly however fast the host is. The serial link has no modem
delay, so it is the quickest of the two. Once a modem call between two gp64
copies is connected, they pass its data to each other directly instead of as
line audio, so a network hiccup delays only the bytes caught in it.

Both links are off by default, and gp64 opens no network sockets until one is
turned on. A link then listens on a TCP port chosen by the system and
advertises it with UDP broadcasts on ports 23517–23520, so the first use may
raise a firewall prompt. The choices are saved for later runs.

- F12 opens the host menu: scaler, fullscreen, mute, recording, serial and
  modem. The menu pauses the program unless a link is connected. Escape or F12
  closes it.
- F11 cycles integer nearest-neighbour, smooth, area and CRT scaling, with 4:3 aspect correction.
- Alt+Enter toggles fullscreen.
- Click inside the window to capture the mouse; Ctrl+F10 releases it.
- Close the window to exit.

## Scripted runs

`--script FILE` runs an emuscru-style script against the program, one command
per line, with `#` comments. The whole script is checked before the program
starts; an unknown command or bad argument is reported with its line number
and gp64 exits with status 1. When the script ends, gp64 exits with status 0.
A failing step, such as a `wait-stable` timeout or an unwritable screenshot,
ends the run with status 1.

- `wait N`: wait N video frames.
- `wait-stable [N]`: wait until three frame hashes taken 10 frames apart agree;
  fail after N frames (default 300).
- `key NAME [FRAMES]`: press and release a key, held for FRAMES frames or by
  default two (`Enter`, `Escape`,
  `Down`, `F1`, `a`, …). `type "text"` types each character, with Shift where needed.
- `mouse-click X Y [left|right|middle]`, `mouse-double-click`, `mouse-down X Y`,
  `mouse-up`: X and Y are pixels of the displayed frame.
- `screenshot [PATH]`: save the displayed frame as PNG; a relative path is
  taken from the current folder, and `{step}` and `{frame}` are filled in.
- `framehash`: log the CRC-32 of the displayed frame.
- `log "text"`, `label: NAME` and `skip-to NAME` (forward only).
- `serial on|off` and `modem on|off`: switch the F12 menu's link for this run
  only; the saved choice is unchanged. Two scripted copies with the same link
  on find each other as from the menu.
- `launch`, `status`, `speed`, `perf-begin` and `perf-end` are accepted and
  ignored; gp64's own command line chooses the program.

Every step is written to the diagnostics log under `gp64::script`. Steps run
only while the program runs, so the F12 menu pauses the script too, and the
keyboard and mouse still work alongside it.

## Limits

The CPU runs real-mode DOS programs through an interpreter. Its rate adjusts
automatically to the fastest sustainable host throughput while timers, video
and audio retain normal emulated timing. Saved CPU speed settings from older
versions are ignored. Conventional memory
and XMS are provided; EMS and DPMI are not. VGA supports standard text and
256-colour modes, including mode 13h and Mode X. The gameport has no controller
attached. AdLib percussion is currently inert.

Sound Blaster support is limited to FM audio and a minimal DSP interface;
digitised audio playback is not emulated. Choose AdLib or PC speaker for audio.
MT-32, GUS, CMS, EMU8000 and MPU synthesis are not emulated. Win16, Win32, other
machines, SVGA chipsets, composite CGA, PCI, ATA/ATAPI, NE2000 networking, JIT
compilation, gamepads, emulator netplay and save states are outside this version.
Menu preferences persist in the user's configuration folder. Only a host folder
can be mounted, not disk or ISO images.

A diagnostics log is kept as `gp64.log` in the user's local data folder
(`%LOCALAPPDATA%\gp64` on Windows, `~/Library/Application Support/gp64` on
macOS). It records serial and modem link changes and the modem's AT commands
and results. Once it reaches 4 MB it becomes `gp64.old.log` and a new log
starts, so the pair stays small. `RUST_LOG` (for example
`RUST_LOG=gp64::hw::serial=debug`) changes how much it records.

## Build from source

Install a current stable Rust toolchain and the platform's native C/linker tools.
On Linux, the window and audio dependencies require development packages for
ALSA and the X11/Wayland libraries selected by winit and softbuffer.

```sh
cargo build --release --locked
cargo test --workspace --locked
cargo test -p gp64-hygiene --locked
```

The executable is `target/release/gp64` (`gp64.exe` on Windows). The intended
platforms are macOS, Windows and Linux, on ARM64 and x86-64. Verification varies
by target; an intended platform is not a guarantee of tested desktop operation.
See [DEVELOPMENT.md](DEVELOPMENT.md) for native tool requirements, checks and
optional external-input tests, and [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md) for security reports.

## Licence and non-affiliation

gp64 is GPL-3.0-or-later; see [LICENSE](LICENSE), [NOTICE](NOTICE) and
[THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md](THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md).

No game files are included. You must own the game. gp64 is not affiliated with or endorsed by the rights holders of F1GP (Formula One Grand Prix).

kylofon-street-rod-2-sdl3-readme-md.text:
# Street Rod 2: The Next Generation — SDL3 port

A faithful native port (C, SDL3) of California Dreams' *Street Rod 2: The Next Generation* (1991),
in the making. Not an emulator. It builds on the engine of the
[Street Rod port](https://github.com/kylofon/street-rod-sdl3), since both games share most of their
code. The original game files are not included: the port reads them from a `Game` folder at run
time.

the launcher, **`Street Rod 2.exe`** (built beside `sr2port.exe` when wxWidgets 3.2 is installed: game folder,

```text

sr2port.exe --game-dir Game              (the original's text menus for video and sound)
```

```text
Game\        the installed DOS game (not in git)
_tools\      junction to Ghidra + JDK (shared with the other ports, not in git)

docs\        manual PDFs/text (not in git)
work\        generated output and DOSBox reference captures (not in git)
site\        local HTML view of PLAN.md with token usage (not in git)
```

vorticoncmdr-re-magicpockets-readme-md.text:
# re-magicpockets

An evidence-grounded HTML5/JS port of **Magic Pockets** (The Bitmap Brothers, DOS 1994), and
the reverse-engineering record it is built from. Vanilla JS and Canvas, no framework. Vite + npm.

## Playing it

**Play it in the browser** (once the repo is public) at <https://vorticoncmdr.github.io/re-magicpockets/>.
The site ships no game data: click **Load folder…** and pick your own copy of the DOS release
(the directory with `GAMEU.EXE`, `INTROU.EXE`, `KLOGOPOU.EXE` and the `data/` files). The files
are read straight from disk and never uploaded.

To run it locally instead, put your copy in `game/` and `data/` (below), start the dev server
and open `http://127.0.0.1:5173/`. The Konami/Renegade logo and the intro play first, then the
world 1 intro and the game.

| Key | Action |
|---|---|
| ←/→ or A/D | walk |
| ↑ or W | jump |
| ↓ or S | down |
| Space, Ctrl or Z | fire |
| digits, arrows, Enter | the level-code screen after a level |

The level-code screen is the original's copy protection (the original asks for a code from the
manual's code wheel). The port pre-enters the expected code, so Enter passes; a wrong code picks
a new prompt, as in the original.

URL options: `?nointro` skips the logo and intro, `?mute` turns the AdLib sound off,
`?level=W.S` starts at world W, sub-level S, `?pick` forces the folder picker, `?debug` shows a
side panel and the status line (tick count, score, unported branches).

This repository ships no game data. For local play:

```bash
npm install
npm run dev          # serves on :5173; game files come straight from game/ and data/
npm run verify       # headless invariant run (needs data/ and game/GAMEU.EXE; no browser)
npm run build:pages  # dist/ holds the playable page and no game data
```

A built page has no `game/` to serve, so it shows **Load folder…** and reads your copy from
disk. Nothing is uploaded, and nothing is ever written back.

## Asset explorer

`viewer.html` (sprites, tiles, maps, pictures, level scripts and MIDI, all decoded in the browser),
`level.html` (the level viewer: map, tile sheet and entity placements) and
`tools/midi-player.html` (the preserved MIDI player; it still needs `npm run extract` output in `build/`) are the explorer pages. The first two read `data/` in the dev server or a picked
folder, so they work on the hosted site too; see `docs/viewer.md` for the controls and `docs/formats/` for the asset formats.

## Project layout

```
game/        your own copy of the game executables (git-ignored, never bundled)
data/        your own copy of the game data files (git-ignored, never bundled)
docs/        subsystem-by-subsystem reverse-engineering findings, with evidence tags
symbols/     Ghidra-derived symbol tables for GAMEU/INTROU/KLOGOPOU
web/core/    isomorphic decoders: RNC, .pak/.pap/.pip/.pin, palettes, LZHUF
web/engine/  the ported game engine, transliterated from the disassembly
web/render/  sprite and tile rendering
web/audio/   the AdLib driver (the original driver bytes run in a tiny 8086 interpreter) and an OPL2 core
web/verify/  the invariant suite behind `npm run verify`
web/play/    the playable page (index.html)
tools/       verify, mutation test, DOSBox capture scripts (attract-capture/, front-capture/, adlib-capture/)
```

`CLAUDE.md` holds the evidence conventions (`[PROVEN]`, `[STATIC]`, `[WF]`, `[UNKNOWN]`) and the
architecture notes. The DOSBox screenshots the sprite and intro checks compare against are not
published; those comparisons are skipped with a note when the files are absent.

## The rule this project runs on

Every claim about the original game says how it was established, and every constant traces to
the disassembly or a captured observation of the real game.

- `[PROVEN]` was executed: decompressed from the shipped bytes, run, or traced live in DOSBox.
- `[STATIC]` was read out of the binary but not confirmed at runtime.
- `[WF]` came from a subagent workflow and is a lead, not a fact.
- `[UNKNOWN]` is not established. Unknowns are registered in `docs/open-questions-history.md`.

Where the port stands in for something not yet decoded, it is labelled in the code and in
`docs/port-plan.md` rather than passed off as the real thing. A check that cannot fail is not
evidence: `tools/lint-checks.mjs` rejects checks where both sides come from project constants.

## Parity with the real game

The method is to port one original function at a time and check each against ground truth
captured from the real game under DOSBox (a Lua script logs the globals and entity records once
per main-loop iteration; the port replays them).

- The whole attract demo (2342 iterations) is reproduced. One-step conformance is entity-exact
  on 2339 of 2339 usable transitions, and a free run, with the engine fed only the first
  captured row, stays exact for 2340 consecutive rows.
- Dozens of live play captures across worlds 1-4, including targeted setups made by poking
  memory (weapons, hurt states, power-ups), replay row for row.
- Sprites match DOSBox video frames pixel for pixel in all four worlds, including the second
  layer over the hero while fire is held (`1000:772C`).
- The AdLib register stream equals a DOSBox capture of the real game, token for token, for all
  82 cues.
- The pre-game screens (Konami/Renegade logo, the intro sequence, the four world intros) equal
  DOSBox video frames by frame hash.

`npm run verify` runs the lint, then the suite, and prints its own totals (currently 401
assertions and 14 notes). `node tools/mutate-engine.mjs` applies plausible mis-ports one at a
time and checks that the suite goes red. A statement counts as `[PROVEN]` only if a mutant of
it is killed, so the survivors it lists are the work queue.

## What is not done

Everything the engine-only fuzz reaches in worlds 1-4 is ported from the disassembly, but only
the branches the live captures exercise are `[PROVEN]`. Still open, among others: the carry-pose
branch of the hero overlay, draw mode 0xb, a few boss and carry/cart handlers, intro sounds, and
sound drivers other than AdLib. See `docs/port-plan.md` and `docs/open-questions-history.md`.

too101-wordpc-disasm-readme-md.text:
# ราชวิถี Word PC version 2.4 — การถอดรหัส Reverse Engineering (เพื่อการศึกษา)

ถอดรหัสโปรแกรม **ราชวิถี Word PC version 2.4** ประมวลผลคำภาษาไทยบน DOS ยุค 1990s
(สร้างโดย น.พ.ชุษณะ มะกรสาร, โรงพยาบาลราชวิถี) กลับเป็น Assembly พร้อมตั้งชื่อฟังก์ชันครบทุกตัว

## ตัวเลขสรุป

| | RWMAIN.EXE | RW.EXE | NLQ.EXE | รวม |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| ขนาดต้นฉบับ | 103,756 ไบต์ | 5,515 ไบต์ | 43,353 ไบต์ | 152 KB |
| คำสั่งที่ถอด | 22,860 | 901 | 9,458 | **33,219** |
| ฟังก์ชันมีชื่อ | 733 | 38 (100%) | 342 (100%) | **1,113** |
| Rebuild รันได้ | ✅ ยืนยันแล้ว | ✅ ยืนยันแล้ว | ✅ ยืนยันแล้ว | 3/3 |

## ไฟล์ในชุดนี้

| ไฟล์ | คืออะไร |
|---|---|
| `ARCHITECTURE.MD` | เอกสารสถาปัตยกรรมครบ 11 หัวข้อ (ระบบย่อยทั้งหมด) |
| `FONT_FORMATS.MD` | รูปแบบไฟล์ฟอนต์ 9 ตระกูล + keyboard layout + driver |
| `THAI_ENCODING_DETECT.MD` | วิธีตรวจจับรหัส KU vs TIS-620 |
| `THAI_CODE_NOTES.MD` | บันทึกการถอดรหัสไทย (KU encoding) |
| `*.LST` | Disassembly listing (พร้อมชื่อ + xref + คำอธิบาย) |
| `*.ASM` | NASM source (assemble กลับได้ขนาดเท่าต้นฉบับ) |
| `*_SUBS.TXT` | ดัชนีฟังก์ชันทั้งหมด |
| `*_STRINGS.TXT` | สตริงไทย KU ถอดเป็น Unicode แล้ว |
| `rw_disasm.py` | ตัวถอดรหัสหลัก (Python + capstone) |
| `mkexe.py` | ตัวสร้าง EXE จาก NASM output |
| `ku_tis_detect2.py` | ตัวตรวจจับรหัสภาษาไทย |
| `BUILD.BAT` | สคริปต์ rebuild ทั้งหมด |

## ระบบที่ถอดแล้ว (ทั้งหมด)

- การเข้ารหัสไทย **KU (เกษตร-ราชวิถี)** — ตารางแปลง KU↔TIS-620
- การแสดงผลไทย **3 ระดับ** (ฐาน/บน/ล่าง) ทั้งจอและเครื่องพิมพ์
- **ตัดคำไทย** ไม่ใช้พจนานุกรม (กฎสระหน้า/วรรณยุกต์/ตัวควบ)
- **Justify engine** + TAB + Area (2 work buffers)
- **Block operations** + ไฮไลต์ (ครบทั้งโหมด column)
- **Pull-down menu** + ระบบแมโครคีย์ + คิวจำลองคีย์
- **CONFIG** 3 ไฟล์ (44+26 คำสั่ง พร้อมค่า default)
- **Mail merge** อ่าน dBASE (.DBF) โดยตรง
- **ฟอนต์ 9 ตระกูล** (.CSL/.NLQ/.LQ/.LQ1/.FONTA/.FONTS)
- **Render engine 16 variants** (italic/reverse/condensed/enlarge)
- **แป้นพิมพ์ไทย** 2 layouts (เกษมณี + ปัตตะโชติ)
- **Printer driver** (ESC sequences + sub/superscript/enlarge/underline)

## การใช้งาน

```bash
# ถอดรหัสใหม่ (ต้องมีต้นฉบับ EXE)
python rw_disasm.py RWMAIN    # หรือ RW / NLQ

# Rebuild (ต้องมี NASM)
nasm -f bin RWMAIN.ASM -o RWMAIN.BIN
python mkexe.py RWMAIN

# ตรวจจับรหัสไฟล์ไทย
python ku_tis_detect2.py <file>
```

## ความถูกต้อง

- **NASM rebuild**: ทั้ง 3 ไฟล์ได้ขนาดเท่าต้นฉบับทุกไบต์ + รันได้จริง
- **Header**: ต่าง 0 ไบต์
- **Module**: ต่างเฉพาะ encoding ทิศคำสั่ง (2,995+114+869 ไบต์) ซึ่งพิสูจน์แล้วว่าเป็นคำสั่งเดียวกัน 100% โดย disassemble เทียบทุกจุด

## ลิขสิทธิ์

โปรแกรมต้นฉบับ: ราชวิถี Word PC version 2.4 — เพื่อการศึกษา/อนุรักษ์เท่านั้น
ชุดถอดรหัสนี้สร้างด้วย Python + capstone + NASM

mitrenga-booty-readme-md.text:
![](/images/app-icon-256x256.png)

BOOTY
=====================
The 1984 ZX Spectrum classic, reborn for modern web browsers.

## About
Originally written in 1984 by John F. Cain and published by Firebird Software
for the 48K ZX Spectrum. This is a faithful remake based on the original
ZX Spectrum version — not an emulator or a binary copy.

Jim the cabin boy is below decks on the Black Galleon, collecting the booty
strewn around its holds. The doors are numbered and so are the keys; trap
doors, ghost pirates, rats, parrots and booby-trapped treasure are in the way.
When the last piece is collected, Jim has 45 seconds to find the golden key —
and the next round begins.

The whole game is playable: all the holds, keys and doors, the enemies, the
booby traps, the golden key and the rounds after it, the original's tune and
sounds, LOAD TAPE with all eight blocks of the original cassette, the title
screen with its rolling sea and the hidden *CATCH 20 GOLDFISH* sub game.

Supported:
- keyboard (redefinable keys)
- gamepad
- touchscreen
- PWA application


## Play now
https://booty.remake.free


## Controls
| key | action |
|---|---|
| arrows | walk, climb ladders |
| space | enter a hold door |
| `M` | music on / off |
| `S` | sound effects on / off |
| Esc | pause |

All keys can be redefined in the menu, including the original's
`5 8 7 6 A`.



## Requirements
- PHP 8.1+
- nginx
- MySQL / MariaDB
- Node.js + terser, for building the bundle (`npm i -g terser`)
- es-check, for the ES2018 compatibility gate in `svtool verify` (`npm i -g es-check`)
- Python 3, only for the tools that extract and verify the data of the original


## Install
(`~/` below refers to the project root, not your home directory.)
- clone this repository
- clone library repository https://github.com/mitrenga/svision **next to it** —
  `~/app/svision` is a relative symlink to `../../svision`
- check symlink ~/app/svision
- configure nginx (example: ~/config/nginx.conf)
- create path ~/js with permissions 0777
- create database (script: ~/config/createDB.sql) — without it the menu does not open
- create configuration file ~/config/config.php (example: ~/config/config.php.sample)
- build the production bundle: ~/app/svision/tools/svtool build bundle


## Developer mode
Developer mode is switched in `~/config/config.php` (both settings are optional; without them the app runs in production mode):

```php
$devMode = true;
$devModeName = '.{\"penColor\":\"#000000\",\"bkColor\":\"#fefe00\",\"width\":185}◢◤ ◢◤ ◢◤ ◢◤  DEVELOPER MODE ◢◤ ◢◤ ◢◤ ◢◤';
```

`$devMode` values:
- `true` — development: JS sources are served directly instead of the bundle and the service worker is unregistered/bypassed
- `['serviceWorker' => true]` — development, but the service worker stays enabled (for testing SW behavior against a built `js/` deploy)
- `false` or not set — production: minified bundle + service worker

`$devModeName` is a label rendered in the top border of the game screen, so a development instance is recognizable at a glance. Set it to `false` (or leave it empty) to hide the label. The value is either plain text, or text prefixed with `.{...}` — a JSON object whose properties are applied to the label's TextEntity, typically:
- `penColor` — text color
- `bkColor` — background color
- `width` — label width in game pixels (the text is centered inside it)

The config is written into a double-quoted JavaScript string, so quotes inside the JSON prefix must be escaped as `\"` (see the example above).

In developer mode the frame rate and the state of the controls are shown in
the border, not over the game screen.


## Build & tooling
The `svtool` CLI (`~/app/svision/tools/svtool`) builds and checks the deploy. Run it from the project root:
- `svtool build bundle` — minified production bundle `js/bundle.<version>.min.js` (requires terser)
- `svtool build debug-bundle` — the same concatenation left unminified, `js/bundle.<version>.js`, for debugging on a device whose console cannot be opened
- `svtool verify` — check the `js/` deploy is complete, matches the current sources, and stays within ES2018 (authoritative via es-check if installed, otherwise a heuristic scan)
- `svtool info` — show the app version, deploy state and the most recent database records
- `svtool clean` — remove everything generated from `js/`

Optional — run `svtool` from anywhere and enable bash completion (adjust the path to your svision clone):
- `sudo ln -s /path/to/svision/tools/svtool /usr/bin/svtool`
- `sudo ln -s /path/to/svision/tools/svtool-completion.bash /etc/bash_completion.d/svtool`

Open a new shell afterwards, then run `svtool <command>` from any project root.

Production serves the bundle; in development, with no bundle built, the sources under `app/` are served and loaded one by one through dynamic `import()`.


## Game data
All the data of the game are in one file, `data/global.json`, in sections
(`holds`, `sprites`, `panel`, `texts`, `memory`, `sounds`, `title`, `tape`,
…) described in [data/README.md](data/README.md). The server sends them to
the application in a single request (`db/appData.php`). Each section is
written by one tool from `tools/`, never by hand, so the game runs from this
repository as it is.

Regenerating or verifying the data needs the original tape image, which is
copyrighted and **not part of this repository**. It goes to
`sources/tape/Booty.tzx`: the Firebird 1984 release as archived by World of
Spectrum / Spectrum Computing (`pub/sinclair/games/b/Booty.tzx.zip`),
46 106 bytes, SHA1 `1a325b309ccae2dd4e2b54b48fc082574ca852ad`. The tools need
Python 3 with the SkoolKit vendored in svision, and Node.js for the `*.mjs`
tools, which load the game's own code from `app/`.


## Repository layout
| path | contents |
|---|---|
| `app/` | the game — ES modules; the workers are classic scripts |
| `data/` | the data extracted from the original (`global.json`) |
| `tools/` | extraction (`dump*`, `mk*`), recording (`trace*`) and verification (`match*`) tools |
| `db/` | PHP endpoints: game data, hall of fame, statistics |
| `config/` | nginx, database, bundle configuration |
| `images/` | icons, poster, cover |


## Credits
- **Booty** © 1984 John F. Cain, published by Firebird Software. This is an
  unofficial fan remake, not affiliated with the rights holders.
- ZX Spectrum ROM © Amstrad plc, used unmodified for the original's noise
  generator; Amstrad permits its redistribution for non-commercial use.
- Built on the [svision](https://github.com/mitrenga/svision) library.


## License
The remake's source code is licensed under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0, see the
[LICENSE](LICENSE) file. The license does not cover the original game — its
graphics, texts, music and the data extracted from it belong to their
authors.

`$devModeName` is a label rendered in the top border of the game screen, so a development instance is recognizable at a glance. Set it to `false` (or leave it empty) to hide the label. The value is either plain text, or text prefixed with `.{...}` — a JSON object whose properties are applied to the label's TextEntity, typically:
- `penColor` — text color
- `bkColor` — background color
- `width` — label width in game pixels (the text is centered inside it)

The config is written into a double-quoted JavaScript string, so quotes inside the JSON prefix must be escaped as `\"` (see the example above).


## Build & tooling
The `svtool` CLI (`~/app/svision/tools/svtool`) builds and checks the deploy. Run it from the project root:
- `svtool build bundle` — minified production bundle `js/bundle.<version>.min.js` (requires terser)
- `svtool build debug-bundle` — the same concatenation left unminified, `js/bundle.<version>.js`, for debugging on a device whose console cannot be opened
- `svtool verify` — check the `js/` deploy is complete, matches the current sources, and stays within ES2018 (authoritative via es-check if installed, otherwise a heuristic scan)
- `svtool info` — show the app version, deploy state and the most recent database records
- `svtool clean` — remove everything generated from `js/`

Optional — run `svtool` from anywhere and enable bash completion (adjust the path to your svision clone):
- `sudo ln -s /path/to/svision/tools/svtool /usr/bin/svtool`
- `sudo ln -s /path/to/svision/tools/svtool-completion.bash /etc/bash_completion.d/svtool`

Open a new shell afterwards, then run `svtool <command>` from any project root.

Production serves the bundle; in development, with no bundle built, the sources under `app/` are served and loaded one by one through dynamic `import()`.


## License
See the [LICENSE](LICENSE) file.
