# Mad Nitro Go

A Go/Ebitengine conversion of **The Nitro-Intro**, released by **Mad of DMA**
in February 1989, using Demo Construction Kit **v1.0.13**. The bitmap font is
credited to **Ming**.

<!-- Project showcase -->
## Screenshots

[![Colorful scrolltext crossing rainbow rasters above the DMA logo](docs/media/screenshot-1.png)](docs/media/screenshot-1.png)

Colorful scrolltext crossing rainbow rasters above the DMA logo.

## Video

[![Animated preview of Mad Nitro Go](docs/media/preview.gif)](https://github.com/olivierh59500/go-mad-nitro/raw/refs/heads/main/docs/media/preview.mp4)

**[Watch or download the 24-second MP4 preview with sound](https://github.com/olivierh59500/go-mad-nitro/raw/refs/heads/main/docs/media/preview.mp4)**

This preview is captured from the Go production.

The animated image is silent; the MP4 includes the soundtrack.

<!-- End project showcase -->

## Production notes

```sh
go run ./cmd/nitro
go run ./cmd/nitro -mute
```

Space or Escape closes the intro. The 320 × 240 canvas includes the lower DMA
title outside the usual 200-line screen. The scene advances at 50 Hz and uses
the original bitmap font, message, two scrolling modes, forty-seven vertical
positions, eighteen title frames and raster color tables.

DCK's SliceStream handles the eight-pixel font strips and the message's control
markers. Its common Scrolling renderer draws the authored glyph window. The
first mode follows an eighteen-column wave and has a scanline reflection;
the control marker changes to the moving vertical lane. A retained DCK sprite
batch draws the reflection, music meters and lower title. YM channel volumes
control the three meters. The original captured YM6 soundtrack is embedded and
opened through DCK's sound facade.

```sh
go test ./...
go vet ./...
go run ./cmd/nitro -capture captures/preview -frame 150 -frames 1
go run ./cmd/video
```

Video export writes a three-minute 640 × 480 H.264/AAC MP4, a PNG poster and a
JSON report under `recordings/`, with DCK's shared graphics/audio clock. The
website uses a VP9/Opus WebM copy. Drawing performs no GPU pixel readback.

Original production: [Demozoo](https://demozoo.org/productions/124014/).

## Android

```sh
./scripts/run-android.sh --build-only
./scripts/run-android.sh
```

The build uses Java 17, Android SDK 36, NDK 28.2, Ebitengine 2.9.11 and the
included Gradle wrapper. It produces an ARM64 APK in
`android/app/build/outputs/apk/debug/app-debug.apk`. The host initializes Go
rendering and audio after the Android context is available, preserves landscape
orientation and keeps the screen awake. Android Back closes the activity.
The install command requires one authorized USB device; `ANDROID_SERIAL`
can select a specific device. Build products and machine settings stay local.

henols-c64-games-bruce-lee-readme-md.text:
# Bruce Lee

*Bruce Lee* is a single-load C64 action game by Ron J. Fortier. Datasoft published it in 1984, and the title reads "REV.2 BY RJF". Bruce goes through 20 rooms, collects lanterns and fights the Yamo (a green sumo) and the Ninja. A second player can control the Yamo. The way leads to the wizard in room 18 and the "CONGRATULATIONS" room 19. Then the game starts a new, faster loop. This documentation is for three cracks of the game, not for a Datasoft release. The base release is the game file of `releases/saeger.d64`, a crack of October 1984 by Saeger Soft Group. The other two reference files are the TBC and DC cracks of the same image. The user gave the three files, and their earlier history is not known. Nobody examined a Datasoft disk or tape of the game. Thus "identical" on these pages means identical to the SAEGER capture, not to the commercial original. The source in [src/](src/) assembles byte for byte to that capture without the crack, and the rebuild shows the Datasoft title picture at the start.

**Evidence.** **Observed** marks a fact that an emulator run or the coverage of the runs showed. **Code** marks a fact from the code or the image only. **Conclusion** marks an interpretation. An **Observed** or **Code** fact is true for the three cracks. A scenario is named by its file in [tests/](tests/).

## The development

The game image of the three cracks is not a clean assembly. About 6 KB of it is bytes that no code of the game reads. The final source only reserved some areas, for example the actor workspace, the sprite buffers, the screen and the gaps in the music code. The assembler did not write these areas, so the older memory content stayed in them. These bytes include copies of older builds and a part of the assembler source text. They also include a part of the symbol table and the data file of a music editor. The rebuild keeps them out of the game, and the knowledge keeps them in the spaces `bank1` to `bank7`. `tests/leftovers_unused.json` fills each leftover with `$A5` at the entry, and the game runs the same (**Observed**).

**A port from the Atari.** Bruce Lee was first an Atari 8-bit game. `atari_digit_key_codes` in bank1 at `$4CBA` holds the Atari keyboard codes of the keys 0-9. The next table holds the same codes plus the Atari SHIFT bit `$40`. No code reads them, and the C64 game has no digit keys (**Code**). So the authors probably made the C64 version from the Atari source, and a table of the Atari version stayed in it (**Conclusion**). A table that the authors copied from Atari notes can also explain it.

**Source text with Apple II conventions.** `$5900-$59A4` holds 165 bytes of assembler source text: the end of the source file of a room charset, with `* CHAR 97` comment lines and `DFB` lines. The characters have bit 7 set, and the lines end in `$8D`. These are the conventions of Apple II assemblers. The 31 bytes in the text are equal to tiles 96-99 of `room_charset_d` (**Observed**). So the authors typed even the graphics as assembler source, one tile at a time (**Conclusion**).

**The source names of the authors.** `$8B00-$8E7F` in bank2 holds 896 bytes of the symbol table of an older build: 88 entries of a length byte, the name and the value. Two offsets give the final address of each value. The names are short codes, for example PLOFS for the frame offset of an actor and IMGL/IMGH for the image address of a frame. The 46 frame labels have the form action, side, phase and sprite layer, for example ADOWNL11. One entry is the typo ADWONL22. The build never referenced it, and a copy of the frame with the right name is in the final build (**Observed**: byte decode). The frame labels show that the Yamo frames first came after the frames of Bruce, and later moved in front of them (**Conclusion**).

**Older builds.** Pages `$EF-$F1` hold code of an older build, `$C600` higher than where it ran. Its addresses show how the program grew: zero page moved up by 3 bytes, and code moved by `$7D` to `$12E` bytes. The old `check_fight_pair` does not have the test for a fall attack that hit the attacker (**Code**). Older copies of two room charsets, two sprite mask tables, four sound effects and the attract demo recording are also in the image. Each differs a little from the final version, so the authors changed these parts late in the work (**Observed**: byte compares).

**The title tune came from a music editor.** `$E800-$EC8F` was the data file of the MicroPearl music editor by John A. Fitzpatrick, loaded `$A800` higher than the editor made it. In the file, voice 0 of the title tune has a first part of 102 bytes. The game does not use it: the song table points voice 0 102 bytes later. So the authors made the tune shorter with a pointer, not with a new file (**Conclusion**).

**Older screens.** The image holds plain-text versions of "BRUCE LEE", "BY", "RON J FORTIER", "GAME OVER" and "PLAYER" in the message format. No pointer goes to them. The final title and game over screens use logo characters and big letters (**Code**).

**The graphic artist.** The game names only Ron J. Fortier ("REV.2 BY RJF"). The Datasoft title picture also names the graphic artist: "GRAPHIC ART BY KELLY DAY" (**Observed**: the picture of the TBC intro). Only the TBC release holds the picture. The rebuild shows it at the start, without the changes of TBC (see Releases and cracks).

The leftovers show what was in memory when somebody saved the image. They do not tell on which computer the authors worked, or the path of the image to the crackers. The details and their evidence are on [docs/development.md](docs/development.md).

## The copy protection

The game expects a protected loader. Nobody examined that loader, because the three files are cracks. The game code tells that the loader left three marks in memory. These are `$EF` in the data direction register `$00` of the CPU port, `$32` in `$02`, and an RTS at `$0080`. The image also holds a key page at `$CF00-$CFFF`. Its two halves of 32 bytes form key pairs: a byte and the byte `$20` higher. A reset machine has `$2F` in `$00`, and nothing in the program writes `$02` (**Code**). So the game cannot run from a plain load of its file (**Conclusion**).

The game checks these marks and keys in eleven places, in all its parts. Two checks run at the cold start, and one runs on each title screen. Two run in every frame, and three are in the room code of rooms 2, 5 and 10. One runs on each pass of a game. The last two checks compute a value in one place and use it in another place (**Code**). Thus a cracker who removes one check still meets the next one (**Conclusion**).

A check that fails does one of three things (**Code**. **Observed** for checks 4, 5, 9, 10 and 11 in the protection runs):

- **It hangs.** The code branches to itself, or loops inside the interrupt.
- **It destroys.** Two checks wipe memory, and one jumps through the empty I/O area at `$DE00`. The room 10 check cuts the maps of rooms 0, 1 and 5. The game then draws these rooms empty in each later game.
- **It waits.** The two delayed checks move their own operands one key pair further on each footstep of any actor. After 32 footsteps they write a TXS into the code, and the game crashes. The crash comes many seconds after the cause, and this hides the source of the crash (**Conclusion**).

All three releases keep every check. Their relocator sets the loader marks again, and the key page comes with the image. Thus their game passes every check (**Observed**: title, demo and game runs). In the rebuild, the switch `PROTECTION` gives each of the 13 patched places its passing path, with the same registers and flags. The patches of the checks that run often also take the same cycles as the passing path of SAEGER. The default build has it off, and each release build has it on. The details are on [docs/protection.md](docs/protection.md).

## Findings

The facts that a reader does not expect. Each page has more.

- **The copy protection is still in the game, and it is delayed.** Several checks compare marks of the protected loader in zero page and pairs of bytes on the key page `$CF00`. A failed check does not stop the game at once. It changes code step by step. Then [`random_byte` `$1159`](src/irq/interrupt_entry_1131.asm#L45) breaks, the game jumps through `$DE00`, or the game wipes memory or damages the maps of rooms 0, 1 and 5. **Code**. **Observed**: junk on the `$CF00` page breaks the game. See [protection.md](docs/protection.md).
- **A room change can stop the game.** [`draw_room` `$09BC`](src/room/draw_room.asm#L28) switches the screen off and on with a read and a write of `SCROLY`. Each write puts bit 8 of the current raster line into the raster compare line. When both writes come on lines 256-311, the compare line stays above the last line of the frame. Then no raster interrupt comes again, and the game waits for ever. **Observed**: the exit from room 15 to room 13 in `runs/room_change_freeze`. See [interrupts.md](docs/interrupts.md).
- **A knock-out by a fall attack repeats.** After the knock-out, [`apply_fight_ko` `$2C24`](src/actor/fight_hits.asm#L384) jumps back to `apply_fight_hits_fall`. So the damage and the points repeat until the energy wraps to a positive value. **Observed**: in one run the score went from 2000 to 15050, and the Yamo survived with 124 energy. See [combat.md](docs/combat.md).
- **Six rooms write 2 bytes into a contact mask.** The maps of rooms 4, 7, 10, 13, 17 and 18 decode to 442 cells instead of 440. The two extra cells write `$80` to `$9010-$9011`, a mask of Bruce's frames. **Observed** in the room runs. See [rooms.md](docs/rooms.md).
- **A new top score moves the next extra fall to 171072 points.** [`update_high_score` `$3184`](src/game/score.asm#L65) copies 4 bytes to `top_score`, and the 4th byte, the raster split index in `$44`, lands in `bonus_fall_first_score`. **Observed** in 7 of 7 stores. See [main_loop.md](docs/main_loop.md).
- **Extra falls come late.** The extra-fall test compares the score with the limit byte by byte, not as one 24-bit number. **Code**. See [main_loop.md](docs/main_loop.md).
- **The random table is filled and never read.** The game fills `random_table` at `$0200`. But `init_game_variables` clears its pointer, so `random_byte` reads zero page and the stack page instead. In the demo it returns 1. **Observed**. See [startup_title.md](docs/startup_title.md).
- **The right-handed key is R.** The title keys L/R and shift-L/shift-R set the joystick handedness of port 1 and port 2. **Code**: key code `$11` is matrix column 2, row 1. **Observed**: the R key of the recording `title_options` runs `title_set_joy1_right_handed`. See [startup_title.md](docs/startup_title.md).
- **The S key only switches the title tune.** The sound effects of the game always play. **Code**. See [sound_music.md](docs/sound_music.md).
- **The music has NTSC tuning.** On PAL every note is about 2/3 of a semitone flat. **Code**. See [sound_music.md](docs/sound_music.md).
- **The attract demo ends at its first lost fall.** It reads 569 bytes of [`demo_input_stream` `$F300`](src/input/demo_input.asm#L12). **Observed**. See [startup_title.md](docs/startup_title.md).
- **Unused exits and a closing exit.** Six entries of the exit tables have no marker in any room. After Bruce defeats the wizard, a tile overwrites the marker of the way back to room 17. **Code**. **Observed** for room 6. See [game_flow.md](docs/game_flow.md).
- **The fourth charset is the wizard flash.** [`room_charset_d` `$9C00`](src/graphics/room_charset_d.asm#L8) becomes `charset_wizard_flash` at `$B800`. Only the defeat of the wizard selects it. **Code**. See [graphics.md](docs/graphics.md).
- **A cracker changed message `$62`.** [`msg_presents` `$4770`](src/text/messages_rooms.asm#L322) reads "DIABOLO  PRESENTS" in the SAEGER release and "DATASOFT PRESENTS" in the TBC and DC releases. No code prints the message. **Observed**: byte compare of the releases. See [releases.md](docs/releases.md).
- **Someone saved the SAEGER image from a game that ran.** The image holds the music state of a tune. It also holds a `$55` of the KERNAL RAM test at `$9B00`, in the source of a room charset. TBC and DC have the bytes from before any run. **Observed**: byte compare and a watchpoint on `$9B00`. **Conclusion**: a dump after a reset. See [releases.md](docs/releases.md).
- **The DC release has no demo input.** Its packed file ends at `$F200`, so the attract demo gives Bruce no input and ends at his first lost fall. **Observed**. See [releases.md](docs/releases.md).
- **Only one crack kept the title picture.** The Datasoft title picture is only in the TBC release, with a crack text in it and simplified colours. The game itself never shows it. **Observed**. A preservation project needs the TBC file for the picture. See [releases.md](docs/releases.md).
- **No cheat or trainer.** `falls_left` decreases only when Bruce loses a fall. It also decreases by 5 when a player-controlled Yamo stays idle too long. The room 16 bonus adds falls. No release adds a trainer. **Code**. **Observed**: byte compare of the releases. See [protection.md](docs/protection.md).

## How the program works

The game is one block of code and data that fills almost all of the 64 KB. The cold start builds the data that the image does not hold. It makes double-height charsets from the ROM font and from the four room charsets. It also makes a contact mask for each pose of the actors. These buffers overwrite their own sources, so the cold start can run only once. Then the title screen runs as a loop of its own. It shows a menu, and after a pause it plays an attract demo from a recorded input stream.

A game is a series of rooms. The game draws each room once from a packed map. Then the code of the room changes it: lanterns disappear, passages open and traps move. The main loop sets the pace of the play. One pass reads the keys, spawns the enemies, runs the room and tests the contacts. It then moves Bruce, the Yamo and the Ninja through their action states and builds their sprites. A pass waits for 3 frames of the interrupt. So the game logic runs at most 50 / 3, about 17, times a second on PAL. The interrupts do the work of each frame. They make the raster splits for the status line, the room charset and the colour bands. They also run the timers, the joysticks and the sound effects.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
  D["Data: room maps and tables, charsets, sprite frames, messages, music, demo input"]
  C["Cold start (once): font copy, double-height charsets, contact masks"]
  T["Title screen and menu"]
  A["Attract demo"]
  M["Main loop: one pass every 3 frames or more"]
  R["Draw the room on each room change"]
  I["Interrupt: every frame"]
  D --> C --> T
  T --> A --> T
  T --> M
  M --> R --> M
  M -- "F1, game over" --> T
  I -- "raster splits, timers, joysticks, sound" --> M
```

1. **The cold start runs once.** [`cold_start` `$0400`](src/game/cold_start.asm#L22) copies the ROM font to `$8800` and expands the four room charset sources at `$9000-$9FFF` into double-height charsets. `build_contact_masks` then builds the contact masks over the charset sources, so the cold start cannot run a second time. (**Code**. [startup_title.md](docs/startup_title.md))
2. **The title is a loop of its own.** [`title_menu_loop` `$08B1`](src/game/title_menu.asm#L14) reads the option keys and the fire button of port 1. After 2400 frames it starts the attract demo. F7 or fire starts a game. (**Observed** in the recordings `title_options` and `demo`)
3. **A room is drawn once and then changed by code.** [`draw_room` `$09BC`](src/room/draw_room.asm#L28) decodes the room map and runs the init handler of the room. Everything that moves or opens later is done by the frame handler of the room, once in each pass. ([rooms.md](docs/rooms.md))
4. **The main loop sets the pace of the game.** One pass of [`main_loop` `$1BC2`](src/game/game_main_loop.asm#L23) runs the keys, the enemy spawns, the room handler and the contact tests. Then it runs the input and the action of each actor, and the sprite builder. It then waits for `frame_countdown`. The interrupt counts this variable down from 3, once in each frame. (**Observed**. [main_loop.md](docs/main_loop.md))
5. **The interrupts set the picture in every frame.** [`irq_entry` `$1103`](src/irq/interrupt_entry.asm#L10) jumps through `irq_vector` to the next raster handler of a chain. In a game, the chain sets the status line, the room charset and the colour bands. `frame_update` runs the timers, the joysticks and the sound effects. ([interrupts.md](docs/interrupts.md))
6. **The actors go through a state machine.** The input of an actor picks an action. The input is a joystick, the computer AI or the demo stream. [`actor_action_step` `$1C5B`](src/actor/actor_step.asm#L21) moves the actor through its states. `select_actor_pose` picks the pose, and `build_actor_sprites` draws the pose into the sprite buffers. ([actors.md](docs/actors.md), [graphics.md](docs/graphics.md))

The flow of a player through the game:

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
  state "Title screen" as Title
  state "Attract demo" as Demo
  state "PLAYER n screen" as Turn
  state "Room play" as Play
  state "Room change" as Enter
  state "Fall lost" as Lose
  state "Game over" as Over
  state "Room 19: congratulations" as End
  [*] --> Title: cold start
  Title --> Demo: 2400 frames
  Demo --> Title: key, fire or first lost fall
  Title --> Turn: F7 or fire on port 1
  Turn --> Play: room 0
  Play --> Enter: exit touched
  Enter --> Play
  Play --> Lose: Bruce dies
  Lose --> Turn: falls left
  Lose --> Over: no falls left
  Over --> Title
  Play --> End: wizard defeated
  End --> Play: next loop, room 0
  Play --> Title: F1
```

The order of the rooms and the conditions that open each way are on [game_flow.md](docs/game_flow.md). Each room is described on [rooms_catalogue.md](docs/rooms_catalogue.md).

## The pages

| Page | Content |
|---|---|
| [docs/startup_title.md](docs/startup_title.md) | **Start-up and title.** The start screen with the title picture, and the cold start. The title screen and its menu, the attract demo, the start of a game and the PLAYER n screen. |
| [docs/main_loop.md](docs/main_loop.md) | **The main loop.** One pass of the game and the game keys. Pause and idle, the status line, the score and extra falls. The loss of a fall, the player switch and game over. |
| [docs/interrupts.md](docs/interrupts.md) | **The interrupt chain.** The IRQ entry and its vector, the raster handlers of the title, PLAYER and game screens, and the work of each frame. |
| [docs/game_flow.md](docs/game_flow.md) | **The game state machine.** The whole program as one state machine, two-player turns, the next game loop, and the map of the 20 rooms from the exit tables. |
| [docs/rooms.md](docs/rooms.md) | **Rooms: data and code.** The room tables, the packed map format, how a room is drawn, the room handlers, lanterns, passages, hazards and the map overflow bug. |
| [docs/rooms_catalogue.md](docs/rooms_catalogue.md) | **The 20 rooms, one by one.** The picture, the data, the setup, the behaviour and the exits of each room. |
| [docs/actors.md](docs/actors.md) | **The actors.** Bruce, the Yamo and the Ninja: their data, spawning, input, the computer AI, the action state machine, movement and poses. |
| [docs/combat.md](docs/combat.md) | **Combat and collision.** Sprite collisions, the background contact test, hits, damage, energy, knock-outs and points. |
| [docs/graphics.md](docs/graphics.md) | **Graphics.** The VIC bank, the double-height tiles, the charsets, the colours and raster splits, the sprite frame format and the double-buffered software sprites. |
| [docs/text_messages.md](docs/text_messages.md) | **Text and messages.** The message format and its printer, the status line, the big banners and all 101 messages. |
| [docs/sound_music.md](docs/sound_music.md) | **Sound and music.** The music player and its stream format, the title tune, the three sound-effect players, the request priorities and the 15 effects. |
| [docs/dispatch_tables.md](docs/dispatch_tables.md) | **Dispatch.** How the program chooses code at run time: vectors, RTS tables, compare chains and computed jumps. |
| [docs/protection.md](docs/protection.md) | **Copy protection.** The delayed protection checks that are still in the game, and the switch that turns them off. |
| [docs/development.md](docs/development.md) | **The development.** What the leftovers in the image tell about how the game was made. |
| [docs/releases.md](docs/releases.md) | **Releases and cracks.** The three cracks compared byte by byte, what each crack changed, and the switches that give each release. |

## Releases and cracks

Three cracks of the game are in the project, in `releases/`. The user gave them, and nobody knows where they were before. All three come from one cracked image. Their game bytes are the same, except for the traces below.

| Label | File | SHA-256 of the PRG file |
|---|---|---|
| SAEGER (base) | `releases/saeger.d64`, file `BRUCE LEE` (`releases/bruce_lee.prg`) | `032fb72523f73a0c9e755809c71bd6072709e42b119deb443b119ca392fb7590` |
| TBC | `releases/bruce_lee_tbc.prg` | `0ed44d52101414928872eddbe1220427f90cbaf129aa41b3d81ba18909b1d597` |
| DC | `releases/danish.d64`, file `BRUCE LEE   (DC)` (`releases/bruce_lee_dc.prg`) | `331fe97e73f8c77624242b4da3029efcb9199ffa184d6cd95220a60311efdaf4` |

- **SAEGER.** Saeger Soft Group, October 1984. It adds an intro that waits for SPACE, a mover and a relocator. The file is not packed. Its game bytes are different from TBC in 76 bytes: message `$62`, the byte at `$9B00` and the music state.
- **TBC.** It adds an intro with the Datasoft title picture, a mover and the same relocator. The file is not packed. It changed no byte of the game.
- **DC.** Danish Crackers, "DC-011/P". It adds an intro and the same relocator, and TCS-CRUNCH packs the file. It changed no byte of the game, but the file does not hold the demo input.

No crack removed a copy protection check. The common relocator writes again the marks of the protected loader (**Observed**: the byte compare, and runs of the title, the demo and the game).

**SAEGER: the edit of another cracker.** [`msg_presents` `$4770`](src/text/messages_rooms.asm#L322) reads "DIABOLO  PRESENTS" in SAEGER and "DATASOFT PRESENTS" in TBC and DC (**Observed**: a byte compare of the releases). No code prints this message (**Code**). Thus a cracker who signed as Diabolo edited the image first, and SSG released that copy later (**Conclusion**). The text identifies a copy of the SAEGER line. The switch `CRACK_DIABOLO` gives the text in the rebuild.

**SAEGER: a dump of a game that ran.** The music variables of SAEGER hold the state after a tune. TBC and DC hold the values from before a run (**Observed**: a byte compare). `$9B00` holds the `$55` of the KERNAL RAM test. Thus somebody reset a running game and saved its memory (**Conclusion**). The game writes each music byte before it reads it, so the music state changes nothing (**Code**. **Observed**: a compare of 900 frames). But [`build_double_height_font` `$4892`](src/room/draw_helpers.asm#L51) reads `$9B00` at the cold start (**Observed**: a watchpoint). Thus SAEGER builds character `$60` of the wizard charset with a different top row. The switch `FIX_RAM_TEST_BYTE` gives the clean byte.

**SAEGER and TBC: tape tools in memory.** The two captures hold the same tape turbo tools at `$FE00-$FFF9`, and DC does not hold them (**Observed**: a byte compare). The game does not use them (**Observed**: `tests/leftovers_unused.json`). Thus the image of SAEGER and TBC went through a machine with a tape turbo (**Conclusion**).

**DC: the demo input is lost.** The packed DC file holds the game only up to `$F200`. Thus [`demo_input_stream` `$F300`](src/input/demo_input.asm#L12) holds the RAM content of the machine: zeros and `$FF` (**Observed**: a byte compare). In the DC release, the attract demo gives Bruce no input. The demo stops at his first lost fall (**Observed**: a run of the DC release). Do not use the DC file as the source of the demo input.

**TBC: the title picture.** Only the TBC intro holds the Datasoft title picture. TBC wrote "CRACKED BY TBC" into the bitmap and gave each cell the same screen colours (**Observed**: a run of the TBC intro). The game itself never shows the picture. A preservation project needs the TBC file for the picture. The rebuild shows the picture as its start screen, without the changes of TBC (see "The start screen" below).

The details, the hashes of the disk images and each different byte are on [releases.md](docs/releases.md).

## The rebuild

**The base release.** The knowledge holds the memory of the SAEGER release when it gets to [`cold_start` `$0400`](src/game/cold_start.asm#L22). It holds only the game: 24 segments from `$03FF` to `$FFFF` (40,075 bytes). The capture leaves out these parts:

- the crack at `$A000-$A9FF`: a copy of the relocator and duplicated pages
- the encoded last stage of the protected loader at `$033C-$03FE`
- 28 leftover blocks of the development and the release, and the 10 leftover ranges of the source

The scenarios `tests/crack_leftover_a000.json`, `tests/crack_leftover_033c.json` and `tests/leftovers_unused.json` show that the game uses none of them (**Observed**).

**The entry state.** The game needs the marks of the protected loader. The relocator of each crack sets them again: `$00` = `$EF`, `$02` = `$32`, an RTS at `$0080`, and `warm_start_flag` = 0. They stay in the entry state. `build/clean_loader.prg` copies the segments into place, sets the entry state of the capture and jumps to `cold_start`. The emulator check of c64-source verified it.

**The start screen.** `build/clean_loader.prg` first shows the Datasoft title picture. Then it waits for a key, or for the fire button of joystick port 1 or 2. The picture comes from the TBC intro: the knowledge holds a capture of the intro at `$0872` in the space `loading`. The switch `CRACK_TBC_PICTURE` of that space holds the changes of TBC: the text "CRACKED BY TBC" and the light blue Chinese name. Its default is 0, so the loader shows the clean picture. The clean cells come from a screenshot of the picture that the user gave, through `src/title_picture.kla` of commit a67158a. Nobody examined a Datasoft file of the picture (**Observed**: the loader check and a byte compare in memory). An older capture of the same intro stays in space bank8 as history. The loader does not use it. Set `START_SCREEN = 0` in `src/config.asm` to start the game at once.

**The leftovers.** No code uses 122 bytes of code and data in 14 ranges (**Observed**: `generate` of c64-re-tools 2.7.0-rc.1 and the test `leftovers_unused`). Examples are an RTS that no code reaches, the unused copy `inc_pointer_06_copy` and the unreachable `unused_jump_reset_vector`. The source keeps them in the files `src/leftovers/leftover_xxxx.asm`. The default build and `build/clean_loader.prg` do not have them, and each release build has them. The switch `LEFTOVERS` in `src/config.asm` puts them in.

**The switches.** `src/config.asm` holds the value of each switch. Change a value there, then build again. `src/switches.asm` holds the value of each switch for each release. The default build is the clean game.

| Switch | Kind | Default | Releases with it on | What it changes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `PROTECTION` | protection | 0 | SAEGER, TBC, DC | the copy protection checks |
| `CRACK_DIABOLO` | crack | 0 | SAEGER | "DIABOLO  PRESENTS" in message `$62` |
| `FIX_RAM_TEST_BYTE` | fix | 1 | TBC, DC | `$0F` in place of the `$55` of the RAM test at `$9B00` |
| `RUN_STATE` | change | 0 | SAEGER | the music state of a run in `$E100-$E86C` |

**The builds.** From the project folder, with the c64-assembler skill:

- `build/clean_loader.prg` is the clean game with the start screen, ready to run. Start the game with this file. `source.ts generate --out src --loader` makes it again. `src/loader.asm` is the packed form, so do not build it alone.
- `assembler.ts build src main.asm --out build/bruce_lee.prg` gives the clean game without a loader.
- `assembler.ts build src main.asm --release SAEGER --compare --out build/bruce_lee_SAEGER.prg` checks the SAEGER build against the bytes of SAEGER in the knowledge. `--release TBC` and `--release DC` check the other releases. Each release build gives its capture byte for byte: SAEGER in all 24 segments, TBC and DC in their 23 segments. The compares include only the captured game. They leave out the crack, the loader stage at `$033C-$03FE` and the leftover blocks.

**The evidence files.** The release files are in `releases/`. The folder `original/` holds the `image.json` of four old captures and a copy of the TBC file. The knowledge gives these files as evidence of old revisions, so they stay. [tests/README.md](tests/README.md) tells more.

**The tests.** Nine recordings in [tests/recordings/](tests/recordings/) play parts of `releases/bruce_lee.prg`, the SAEGER file: the title and its options, the demo and the game keys. Other recordings play two players, a player Yamo, a game over and all 20 rooms. Each recording replays on `build/clean_loader.prg` with the same game state at each checkpoint, 11845 checkpoints in all (**Observed**, c64-re-tools 2.7.0-rc.1). The replays pin the stack page, because `random_byte` reads it. Seven scenarios and run files test what a replay cannot test:

- `leftovers_unused`, `crack_leftover_a000` and `crack_leftover_033c` put junk in the unused blocks of the SAEGER file, and the game runs the same.
- `no_protection` destroys the protection data of the default build and compares it with the TBC release.
- `start_screen`, `start_screen_fire` and `start_screen_waits` test the start screen of the loader.

[tests/README.md](tests/README.md) gives the conditions of each test and the parts that it does not compare. [tests/PLAYTEST.md](tests/PLAYTEST.md) is the checklist for a human playtest.

## Still open

These questions come up on more than one page. Each page lists its own questions at its end.

- **Some code never ran.** The coverage of all runs misses 763 instructions in 121 ranges. Examples are parts of the wizard defeat, some room events and several protection paths. The source marks each range with `; not executed`, and `.c64-re-tools/local/generated/src/not_executed.json` lists them. Git does not keep that file: `generate` writes it again. Runs that reach these paths can close the gaps.
- **What some room pieces are in game terms.** The sliders, the runners and some graphic messages have names that come from their place and use. See [rooms.md](docs/rooms.md).
- **The warm-start flag.** [`warm_start_flag` `$03FF`](src/game/cold_start.asm#L7) must be 0, and nothing writes it. The protected loader may have had a restart path. See [protection.md](docs/protection.md).

## The reference

[docs/reference/index.md](docs/reference/index.md)

# Combat: hits, energy and the end of a bout

A bout in Barbarian ends in one of two ways only. One fighter loses all 12 units of energy, or a sword cuts off his head. The game does not use the sprite collision of the VIC-II to find a hit. In each pass, it compares two pose numbers: the pose of the attacker and the pose of the defender. A table gives one record for each pair of poses that can touch. The record gives the distances where the blade hits and the reaction of the defender. It also gives the sound, the energy loss, the red hit sprite and the points. After a death or a decapitation, the winner makes his winner move, and a green goblin drags the body out of the arena. This page tells how the code does each step in build V 05 05 87 of Part 2.

**Conventions.**
- Addresses are C64 addresses. Names are the names of the knowledge.
- A *pass* is one run of `main_loop`. The main loop has no frame wait, so a pass takes about 10 frames. Each fighter shows one pose for each pass.
- A *pose* is the number in `fighter_pose` (`$00-$5B`). A *move* is the number in `fighter_move`, with bit 7 set: `$8D` is move `$0D`.
- The *attacker* is the fighter that the code tests for a hit. The *defender* is the other fighter.
- An *attack pose* is one of the 12 poses in `attack_poses`. Only these poses can hit.
- The *distance* is the difference of the two `fighter_x` values, in columns of 8 pixels, without a sign.
- A *hit record* is one of the 39 entries of 4 bytes in `hit_records`.
- Fighter 0 is player 1 (port 2). Fighter 1 is the computer in a one-player game of Part 2.
- **Observed** marks a fact that a run showed. **Code** marks a fact from the code only. **Conclusion** marks an interpretation.

## How it works

~~~mermaid
flowchart TB
  A["Each pass: check_hits"] --> B{"Bout over, turn, walk-in, set-up or final stage?"}
  B -- yes --> Z["No test in this pass"]
  B -- no --> C["Attacker = fighter 1, then fighter 0"]
  C --> D{"Attacker in an attack pose? (find_attack_pose)"}
  D -- no --> N["Next attacker"]
  D -- yes --> E["Next entry of the hit list of that pose"]
  E --> F{"Entry for the defender pose?"}
  F -- "no, end of list" --> N
  F -- yes --> G{"Distance bit set in the hit record?"}
  G -- no --> E
  G -- yes --> H["Reaction move, sound and damage (apply_hit_damage)"]
  H --> I["Hit sprite and score"]
  I --> N
~~~

[`check_hits` `$879B`](../src/combat/hits.asm#L6) runs in each pass, after the fighters have their new poses and after `get_fighter_distance`. It does nothing when bit 7 is 1 in one of six flags: `bout_loser`, `turn_request`, `walk_in_active`, `setup_active`, `time_out_active` or `final_stage`. Thus no hit can occur after the end of a bout, while the fighters turn or walk in, or in the final stage (**Code**). The bolts of Drax use other code, see [final_stage.md](final_stage.md).

[`check_attack_hit` `$87B9`](../src/combat/hits.asm#L25) tests one attacker. It does these steps (**Code**):

1. `find_attack_pose` looks for the pose of the attacker in `attack_poses`. When the pose is not an attack pose, the test ends.
2. The index of the attack pose selects a word in `hit_list_ptrs`. The word points to the hit list of that pose: pairs of defender pose and hit record number, with `$FF` at the end.
3. The code reads the list from the start. It skips each entry with another defender pose.
4. At an entry with the defender pose, `get_hit_record` calculates the address of the hit record: `hit_records` + 4 x number.
5. The code calculates the distance again. At a distance of 8 or more, the test ends with no hit.
6. The code takes the bit of the distance from `bit_masks` and does an AND with byte 0 of the record. When the result is 0, the code goes to the next entry of the list (step 3).
7. When the bit is 1, the hit occurs. `apply_hit_damage`, `spawn_hit_sprite` and `add_hit_score` use bytes 1-3 of the record. The test then ends, so an attacker makes at most one hit in a pass.

The code tests fighter 1 first, then fighter 0. It does not look at the facing of the fighters. The distance has no sign, so the same record applies when the defender stands behind the attacker (**Code**). After the turn of the fighters, this case is rare (**Conclusion**).

### The attacks

The 12 attack poses belong to nine moves that the joystick selects. The table gives the joystick for a fighter that stands and faces right. The details of the moves are on [fighters.md](fighters.md). The distances, points and sprites come from the records that most entries of each list use (**Code**).

| Attack pose | Move | Joystick | Distances of most entries | Reaction of the defender | Points | Hit sprite |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `$05`, `$07` | `$83` | fire + up-back | 0 (also 0-1 or 0-2) | `$99` | 50 | effect 1 or 2 |
| `$0C` | `$85` | fire + down (after the crouch `$97`) | 0-2 | `$8D` | 100 | effect 3 |
| `$17` | `$89` | fire + forward | 0-1 | `$8D` | 200 | effect 4 |
| `$1A` | `$87` | fire + back (the move starts with the three poses of the turn) | 0-3, 0-2 or 0-1 | `$8D`, or `$88` (decapitation) | 200, or 500 | effect 6 |
| `$1C` | `$8C` | fire + down-forward | 0 | `$99` | 100 | none |
| `$20` | `$8E` | fire + down-back | 0-2 | `$99` | 100 | effect 5 |
| `$22` | `$8F` | fire + up-forward | 0 | `$99` | 200 | none |
| `$24`, `$25`, `$26` | `$91` | down-forward (the roll) | 0 or 0-1 | `$99` | 0, and no damage | none |
| `$43` | `$8B` | fire + up | 0-2 | `$8D` | 200 | effect 6 |

No record allows a distance above 3. The records 1, 7 and 9 are in no list (**Code**).

The reaction moves are short. Move `$8D` shows the poses `$1D`, `$1E` and `$00`. Move `$99` shows the poses `$4C-$4F`. The record writes the reaction move also into `fighter_move_lock`, so the joystick cannot change the move until its last pose (**Code**). The roll knocks the opponent with move `$99`, but it takes no energy and gives no points (**Code**).

### Clashes and safe poses

Some records have reaction move 0 and damage 0. They play sound 2 (requests `$DA`, `$DB` and `$DC`) and do nothing else. Most of these entries pair an attack pose with the same attack pose: two swords meet (**Conclusion**). An example is `hit_list_00`: the pose `$05` against the poses `$05` and `$07` gives this clash (**Code**).

A defender pose that is not in a list is safe from that attack. The lists have 30-61 entries each. The reaction poses `$1D`, `$1E` and `$4C-$4F`, the death poses `$56`, `$57`, `$21` and `$59`, and the decapitation poses `$11-$14` are in no list. Thus a fighter cannot get a second hit while he shows a reaction pose (**Code**). The crouch pose `$3A` (move `$86`) is not in the list of the attack pose `$1A`, so a crouch protects the neck (**Code**).

### A bug: the second entry for a defender pose

Fourteen list entries repeat a defender pose of the same list. The first entry gives one set of distances, and the second entry gives other distances. An example in `hit_list_00`: pose `$17` with record `$13` (distance 0), then pose `$17` with record `$10` (a clash at distance 1-3) (**Code**).

[`get_hit_record` `$8832`](../src/combat/hits.asm#L96) shifts the record number two times into the high byte of `move_ptr`. The code needs 0 in that byte. `check_attack_hit` writes the 0 only one time, before the first entry. The first matching entry leaves `$C7` or `$C8` there. Thus a second matching entry gets a wrong record address (**Code**):

| Attack pose | Defender poses | Record of the table | Address that the code reads | Bytes there in the release |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `$05` | `$17` | `$10` (clash) | `$E3ED` (`arena2_screen_tail`) | `$98 $98 $98 $98` |
| `$07` | `$17` | `$10` (clash) | `$E7ED` (`arena2_colours_tail`) | `$A7 $F7 $B7 $A7` |
| `$1A` | `$1B`, `$1C` | `$0D` (clash) | `$E7E1` (`arena2_colours`) | `$C5 $20 $FC $FC` |
| `$1A` | `$3F`, `$40`, `$41`, `$42`, `$44`, `$47`, `$4B` | `$0B` (hit, 200) | `$E3D9` (`arena2_screen`) | `$BC $BC $5C $5C` |
| `$20` | `$15` | `$0D` (clash) | `$E7E1` (`arena2_colours`) | `$C5 $20 $FC $FC` |
| `$43` | `$1B`, `$1C` | `$0D` (clash) | `$E3E1` (`arena2_screen`) | `$C0 $5C $50 $B0` |

The bytes come from the bottom row of the screen and the colours of the second arena. Some come from the 24 bytes after them. The scene change does not write these cells. **Conclusion:** the intended clash or hit does not occur. At some distances, these bytes give a hit with wrong numbers. The move can be above `$1D`, and the sound, sprite and score entries can be above the ends of their tables. For example, the attack pose `$1A` against the defender pose `$3F` at distance 2 starts move `$3C`, which has no entry in `move_seq_ptrs`.

No run showed this case. The coverage maps of the recordings mark only the code, so they do not show which records the code read. Build V 05 10 87 keeps the bug. But it adds two checks: no hit on a defender pose of `$5B` or more, and no points for a score entry of 5 or more. **Conclusion:** the authors saw the effects and did not find the cause. The details are on [../../docs/versions.md](../../docs/versions.md).

## Damage and energy

[`apply_hit_damage` `$8845`](../src/combat/hits.asm#L109) uses byte 2 of the record (**Code**):

1. The high nibble selects a triplet in `hit_sounds`. The code writes each byte that is not 0 into `sound_request` of that voice.
2. When the low nibble is 0, the hit takes no energy. Each other value takes exactly 1 unit: the code does a `DEC`, not a subtraction of the nibble.
3. If the corner block of the defender does not play its hit animation, the code starts it. Fighter 0 gets animation 2, and fighter 1 gets animation 3.
4. `fighter_energy` of the defender goes down by 1.
5. At 0 energy, `bout_loser` gets `$80` + the defender, and the defender starts the death move `$9B`.

Each fighter starts a bout with 12 units. `reset_fighter` sets this value. Thus 12 hits with damage kill a fighter, if no decapitation occurs first (**Code**). The recordings `win_bout`, `final_lose` and `final_win` write 1 into the energy of the computer, and one hit then ends the bout (**Observed**).

### The energy bars

[`show_energy_scores` `$82DA`](../src/score/status_line.asm#L62) prints one of the texts `text_energy_00` to `text_energy_12` in each pass. Each text has 2 rows of 6 characters at the top of the screen: column 0 for fighter 0 and column 34 for fighter 1. The characters "(" and ")" draw the two halves of a round symbol. Thus 6 round symbols show 12 units, and each hit removes one half (**Code**).

The corner block is 4 x 4 cells under the energy bar. Its hit animation shows 7 frames, one for each pass, and then stops. A hit during the animation does not start it again, but the energy still goes down (**Code**). The details of the corner animations are on [graphics.md](graphics.md).

### The trainer

The Hotline release puts `JSR $CF20` and a `NOP` at `$8880`, in place of the store to `corner_anim_pos` and the `DEC`. The routine at [`unused_cf20` `$CF20`](../src/data/unused_cf20.asm#L6) does the store and the `DEC` only for fighter 1. Thus player 1 does not lose energy. The switch `TRAINER` builds this patch. It is off in the default build (**Code**). The details are on [../../docs/releases.md](../../docs/releases.md).

## The hit sprites

[`spawn_hit_sprite` `$8896`](../src/combat/hits.asm#L173) uses the high nibble of byte 3 of the record. When it is not 0, the code starts a sprite in the first free slot. The entry in `hit_sprite_effects` gives the animation, the Y position and an X offset (**Code**).

All six entries use the sprite animation `$8A`: one red image for 10 frames, then the sprite stops. Only the position differs. The Y positions are `$9F` to `$C0` (**Code**). **Conclusion:** the red spot shows the blood of the hit, at the head, the body or the legs.

`set_sprite_x` puts the sprite at the column of the attacker x 8 + the offset + `$18`. For an attacker that faces left, the offset becomes `$30` - offset. The search for a free slot always found slot 0 in the recordings. The code that tests the next slot never ran (**Observed**).

## The score

[`add_hit_score` `$88E5`](../src/combat/hits.asm#L225) uses the low nibble of byte 3 of the record. It selects 5 decimal digits in `score_values`: 500, 200, 100 or 50 points. `add_score_digits` adds them to the score text of the attacker, `text_score0` or `text_score1`, one digit at a time with a carry (**Code**).

The score is a text of 5 digit characters. No binary score exists. The computer also gets points for its hits. `init_fighters` clears both scores. The start code and `read_keys` call it, but the end of a bout does not. Thus the score of player 1 grows from bout to bout (**Code**). The time bonus of `add_time_bonus` runs only in a two-player game, and Part 2 has no two-player game. The details are on [game_flow.md](game_flow.md).

## The decapitation

Only the attack pose `$1A` of move `$87` (fire + back) can cut off a head. Its hit list gives the records 4 and 5 for 29 defender poses (**Code**):

- Record 4 at distance 0-2: the stance `$00`, the walk poses `$01-$03` and `$33-$37`, and the poses `$32`, `$48` and `$51-$54`.
- Record 5 at distance 0-1: 14 other poses, for example the poses `$04-$06` of move `$83`.

The idle move `$9A` of a human player shows the poses `$52-$54`. Thus a player who does nothing loses his head when the computer swings at the correct distance (**Code**). The recording `decapitation` shows this: opponent 7 decapitates the idle player (**Observed**).

The record gives the defender move `$88`, sound 3 and 500 points. It takes no energy, so the energy of the defender has no effect (**Code**). In the next pass, [`check_decapitation` `$90F0`](../src/combat/bout_end.asm#L6) finds move `$88` and sets `bout_loser`. It starts three sprites at the position of the defender (**Code**):

| Sprite | Animation | Motion | Y | Conclusion |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | `$80` or `$81` by facing: a turning multicolour image | `$81` or `$82`: an arc in the facing direction of the loser, two smaller bounces with sound `$DF`, then animation `$84` or `$85` without motion | `$9D` | the head |
| 1 | `$83`: one black image | `$83` or `$84`: along the floor, at the speed of the head | `$CD` | the shadow of the head |
| 2 | `$82`: four red images, then the sprite stops | `$80`: no motion | `$9D` | the blood |

`move88_sprite0_anims` holds `$80`, `$81`, `$84`, `$85`, and the code reads only the first two. The head gets `$84` or `$85` later, from its motion. `move88_sprite_x` holds `$18` and `$48` (**Code**).

Move `$88` shows the poses `$11-$14` and then holds `$14`: the body falls (**Conclusion**).

## The end of a bout

### The winner move

[`start_winner_move` `$917B`](../src/combat/bout_end.asm#L83) runs after a death in `check_hits`, and after the start of a decapitation. It writes `bout_winner` and gives the winner one of two moves (**Code**):

- After a decapitation, or at a distance of 2 or more: move `$93`. It shows the poses `$3C` and `$00`, then `$2F-$31` and again `$2F`, and then it holds `$2F`.
- After a death at a distance of 0 or 1: move `$9C`. It shows the poses of move `$8C` (fire + down-forward), and then it starts move `$93`.

The recordings `attract`, `fight` and `win_bout` ran the code of move `$9C`. The recordings `decapitation`, `fight`, `final_lose`, `final_win` and `win_bout` ran the code of move `$93` (**Observed**).

The test of `bout_loser` is at the start of `check_hits`, not between the two attackers. **Conclusion:** both fighters can lose their last unit in the same pass. Fighter 1 hits first and sets `bout_loser` to `$80`. Then fighter 0, still in its attack pose, can hit fighter 1 and set `$81`. Then player 1 wins the bout with 0 energy. Build V 05 10 87 adds a test of `bout_loser` before each attacker. No run showed this case.

### The goblin

![The goblin drags the body away](images/goblin.png)

The green goblin drags the body of the loser out of the throne room. The winner stands at the left (**Observed**).

[`start_goblin` `$91A7`](../src/combat/bout_end.asm#L113) waits until the loser shows the last pose of his fall: `$59` after a death, or `$14` after a decapitation. Then it puts sprites 3 and 4 at X `$27` at the left edge, one above the other. They walk to the right with the animations `$86` and `$87` and the motion `$85`. `goblin_active` gets `$FF` (**Code**).

The raster interrupt calls [`update_goblin` `$9639`](../src/story/goblin.asm#L6) in each frame. It does three tests (**Code**):

1. After a decapitation, when sprite 3 reaches the head (sprite 0), the head and its shadow get new motions. The head flies to the right, and the motion requests sound `$DF` (**Conclusion:** the goblin kicks the head).
2. When sprite 3 reaches the column of the body + 5, the goblin stops for 100 frames with the animations `$88` and `$89`. Then it walks to the right again. `goblin_drags` gets `$FF`, and the code requests sound `$E2`.
3. While bit 7 of `goblin_drags` is 1, the code can add 1 to `fighter_x` of the loser. It does this when sprite 3 is at the edge of a column and in front of the body. The body moves with the goblin.

The code that plays sound `$EB` on three voices in step 1 never ran (**Observed**). The goblin also comes after a death without a decapitation, because `start_goblin` waits for pose `$59` (**Code**).

### Back to the start

[`end_bout` `$83F8`](../src/combat/end_of_bout.asm#L6) waits until the body is at column 40 or more, out of the screen. Then the winner turns with move `$9D` if he does not face his start direction. He walks with move `$82` to his home column, 3 or 28. There, the code resets both fighters, clears the flags of the bout and starts the walk-in (**Code**).

Then the result decides the next step. When the player lost, the game waits 200 frames and starts the demo. When the player won, `opponent_index` goes up by 1, or the final stage starts after opponent 7. The details are on [game_flow.md](game_flow.md) (**Code**).

A one-player bout in Part 2 has no time limit. Only the two-player code reads the bout clock (**Code**). Thus each bout ends with a death or a decapitation.

## The data

### The hit lists

`attack_poses` has the 12 attack poses `$05`, `$07`, `$0C`, `$17`, `$1A`, `$1C`, `$20`, `$22`, `$24`, `$25`, `$26` and `$43`. `hit_list_ptrs` has one word for each, in the same order. The 12 lists fill `$C2EA-$C7AB` (**Code**):

| Byte | Meaning |
|---|---|
| 0 | Pose of the defender. `$FF` ends the list. |
| 1 | Number of the hit record, `$00-$26`. |

### The hit records

`hit_records` at `$C7AC-$C847` has 39 records of 4 bytes (**Code**):

| Byte | Bits | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | bit n | Distance n gives a hit. The table uses only bits 0-3. |
| 1 | all | Reaction move of the defender: `$8D`, `$99` or `$88`. 0: no reaction move. |
| 2 | 7-4 | Entry of `hit_sounds`, 1-4. |
| 2 | 3-0 | 0: no damage. Not 0: the defender loses 1 unit. |
| 3 | 7-4 | Entry of `hit_sprite_effects`, 1-6. 0: no sprite. |
| 3 | 3-0 | Entry of `score_values`, 1-4. 0: no points. |

### The tables that the records select

| Table | Entry | Bytes |
|---|---|---|
| `hit_sounds` | 1 | `$E9`, 0, `$EA`: a normal hit |
| `hit_sounds` | 2 | `$DA`, `$DB`, `$DC`: a clash |
| `hit_sounds` | 3 | `$E1`, `$E1`, 0: a decapitation |
| `hit_sounds` | 4 | `$EE`, `$EE`, 0: the attack pose `$22` |
| `hit_sprite_effects` | 1-6 | animation `$8A`, then Y `$B8`, `$B8`, `$C0`, `$B5`, `$9F`, `$A4` and X offset `$20`, `$30`, `$30`, `$30`, `$28`, `$30` |
| `score_values` | 1-4 | 00500, 00200, 00100, 00050 |

Entry 0 of each table is not used. The sound bytes are tune requests for the three voices. The sound page of this project tells more about them.

## The state machine of the end of a bout

The flags `bout_loser`, `goblin_active`, `goblin_drags` and `walk_in_active` hold the state. `check_hits`, `check_decapitation`, `start_goblin`, `update_goblin` and `end_bout` make the changes.

~~~mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
  state "Fight" as Fight
  state "Death fall (move $9B)" as Death
  state "Head cut (move $88)" as Cut
  state "Loser falls, winner move" as Fall
  state "Goblin walks in" as Walk
  state "Goblin drags the body" as Drag
  state "Winner walks home" as Home
  [*] --> Fight
  Fight --> Death: energy 0
  Fight --> Cut: record with move $88
  Death --> Fall: same pass
  Cut --> Fall: next pass
  Fall --> Walk: loser pose $59 or $14
  Walk --> Drag: goblin at the body
  Drag --> Home: body at column 40
  Home --> [*]: winner at home column, walk-in
~~~

| State | Condition | Next state | Code |
|---|---|---|---|
| Fight | `fighter_energy` of the defender becomes 0 | Death fall | `apply_hit_damage` |
| Fight | a record gives move `$88` | Head cut | `check_attack_hit` |
| Death fall | `bout_loser` bit 7 set after both attackers | Loser falls, winner move | `start_winner_move` |
| Head cut | a fighter in move `$88`, `bout_loser` clear | Loser falls, winner move | `check_decapitation` |
| Loser falls | `fighter_pose` of the loser is `$59` or `$14` | Goblin walks in | `start_goblin` |
| Goblin walks in | column of sprite 3 - 3 = column of the body + 5 | Goblin drags | `goblin_grab_body` |
| Goblin drags | `fighter_x` of the loser is `$28` or more | Winner walks home | `end_bout` |
| Winner walks home | `fighter_x` of the winner is the home column | walk-in of the next bout | `end_bout_reset` |

## The worked example

The recording `win_bout` attacks with fire + down at distance 2. This example decodes that attack against a computer fighter in the stance `$00`. The bytes come from the release (**Code**).

| Address | Table | Index | Bytes | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `$C2C8` | `attack_poses` | 2 | `$0C` | pose `$0C` of move `$85` is attack pose 2 |
| `$C2D6` | `hit_list_ptrs` | 2 | `$C3D2` | the list `hit_list_02` |
| `$C3D2` | `hit_list_02` | entry 0 | `$00 $19` | defender pose `$00`: record `$19` |
| `$C810` | `hit_records` | `$19` | `$07 $8D $11 $33` | the record |
| `$CEA8` | `bit_masks` | 2 | `$04` | the bit of distance 2 |
| `$C84B` | `hit_sounds` | 1 | `$E9 $00 $EA` | requests for voices 1 and 3 |
| `$C860` | `hit_sprite_effects` | 3 | `$8A $C0 $30` | animation `$8A`, Y `$C0`, X offset `$30` |
| `$C87B` | `score_values` | 3 | `$00 $00 $01 $00 $00` | 100 points |

The code does these steps:

1. `$04` AND `$07` = `$04`, not 0: a hit.
2. Byte 1 = `$8D`. The defender gets move `$8D` and `fighter_move_lock` = `$8D`, at step 0.
3. Byte 2 = `$11`. Sound entry 1 writes `$E9` and `$EA` into the requests of voices 1 and 3. The damage nibble is 1, so the energy goes down by 1.
4. Byte 3 = `$33`. Sprite entry 3 puts a red spot at Y `$C0`, the lowest of the six positions. Score entry 3 adds 100 to `text_score0`.

At distance 3, `$08` AND `$07` = 0. The list has no other entry for pose `$00`, so the attack misses. The same attack against pose `$0A`, the first pose of move `$85`, uses record `$1A` (`$03`). It hits only at distance 0 or 1 (**Code**).

## Still open

- **The wrong hit records.** What does the game do when the bug reads a record at `$E3D9`, `$E3E1`, `$E7E1` or `$E7ED`? Run: a fight with fire + back at distance 2 against an opponent in pose `$3F`, with a breakpoint at `check_attack_hit_entry` and a watch on `move_ptr`.
- **The double death.** Can both fighters reach 0 energy in one pass? Run: set the energy of both fighters to 1 and give attacks at the same time.
- **The roll.** Which poses of the computer let a roll knock it at distance 0 or 1? Run: the recording `fight` with a breakpoint at `check_attack_hit_apply`.
- **The clash.** Which sound do the requests `$DA`, `$DB` and `$DC` play? Run: two fighters with the same attack at distance 0-3.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Render Boulder Dash (C64) caves on the console from a 64 KB VICE memory dump.

Two modes:
  live   - print the cave map exactly as it is in RAM ($0850-$0BBF, 40x22),
           i.e. the running game's current state, plus the status values.
  decode - rebuild any of the 20 caves at any level (1-5) the way the game
           does it at cave start ($8AB9):
             $8226 copy the cave record to $2400 and seed the RNG
             $8043 random fill of rows 1-21 (RNG $7085, tables $2418/$241C)
             $85A7 steel border (tile $07, 40x22 outline)
             $8518 draw the object list at $2420 (point/line/box/outline)
           All tables (cave offsets, row table, direction table) are read from
           the dump itself, so nothing game-specific is hard-coded except
           addresses.

Usage:
  bd_cave_render.py DUMP                      # live map of the running game
  bd_cave_render.py DUMP --cave 13 --level 1  # decode cave M, level 1
  bd_cave_render.py DUMP --all                # decode all 20 caves, level 1
  bd_cave_render.py DUMP --diff               # decode the current cave and
                                              # compare it with the live map
Options: --color (ANSI colours), --legend, --hex (tile IDs instead of chars)
"""

import argparse
import sys

# --- addresses (see sessions/boulderdash/*.txt) ------------------------------
MAP_BASE = 0x0850          # live cave map, 40 x 22, row-major
MAP_W, MAP_H = 40, 22
DECODE_BASE = 0x0800       # decoder y coordinates are map row + 2 ($8406 table)
ROW_TABLE = 0x8406         # 2-byte row addresses used by the object decoder
DIR_TABLE = 0x8454         # 8 x 2-byte signed deltas for line directions
CAVE_OFFSETS = 0x5804      # word per cave number: offset from CAVE_DATA
CAVE_DATA = 0x582E
RECORD_LEN = 240           # bytes copied to $2400 by $8246
CAVE_COUNT = 20

# tile ID -> (char, ansi colour, description)
TILES = {
    0x00: (" ", "0", "empty"),
    0x01: (".", "33", "dirt"),
    0x02: ("=", "37", "brick wall"),
    0x03: ("M", "36", "magic wall"),
    0x04: ("X", "90", "exit (closed)"),
    0x05: ("E", "92", "exit (open)"),
    0x07: ("#", "90", "steel wall"),
    0x10: ("o", "97", "boulder"),
    0x14: ("*", "96", "diamond"),
    0x25: ("I", "95", "entrance"),
    0x38: ("@", "93", "player"),
    0x3A: ("a", "32", "amoeba"),
}
RANGES = [  # (lo, hi, char, colour, description)
    (0x08, 0x0F, "F", "91", "firefly (+moved)"),
    (0x11, 0x13, "o", "97", "boulder (moved/falling)"),
    (0x15, 0x17, "*", "96", "diamond (moved/falling)"),
    (0x1B, 0x1F, "%", "31", "explosion -> space"),
    (0x20, 0x24, "$", "94", "explosion -> diamond"),
    (0x26, 0x28, "I", "95", "entrance animation"),
    (0x30, 0x37, "B", "35", "butterfly (+moved)"),
    (0x39, 0x39, "@", "93", "player (moved)"),
    (0x3B, 0x3B, "a", "32", "amoeba (new)"),
]


def tile_info(t):
    if t in TILES:
        return TILES[t]
    for lo, hi, ch, col, desc in RANGES:
        if lo <= t <= hi:
            return ch, col, desc
    return "?", "0", "unknown"


def cave_name(n):
    if 1 <= n <= 16:
        return "Cave " + chr(ord("A") + n - 1)
    if 17 <= n <= 20:
        return "Intermission %d" % (n - 16)
    return "cave #%d" % n


def load_dump(path):
    data = open(path, "rb").read()
    if len(data) != 0x10000:
        sys.exit("%s: expected a 65536-byte RAM dump, got %d bytes" % (path, len(data)))
    return data


def word(mem, addr):
    return mem[addr] | (mem[addr + 1] << 8)


# --- game algorithms ---------------------------------------------------------
def next_random(s1, s2):
    """$7085: s1 = $3F, s2 = $3E. Returns (s1, s2); the game uses s1."""
    t1 = (s1 & 1) << 7
    t2 = (s2 >> 1) & 0x7F
    r = s2 + ((s2 & 1) << 7)
    c = r >> 8
    r = (r & 0xFF) + c + 0x13
    c = r >> 8
    s2 = r & 0xFF
    r = s1 + c + t1
    c = r >> 8
    r = (r & 0xFF) + c + t2
    s1 = r & 0xFF
    return s1, s2


def cave_record(mem, n):
    """$8226: 240 bytes from $582E + word[$5804 + 2n]."""
    start = CAVE_DATA + word(mem, CAVE_OFFSETS + 2 * n)
    return bytes(mem[(start + i) & 0xFFFF] for i in range(RECORD_LEN))


class Decoder:
    def __init__(self, mem):
        self.mem = mem
        # buffer covers $0800-$0BBF (decoder rows 0..23, map rows = y - 2)
        self.buf = bytearray(MAP_W * (MAP_H + 2))
        self.dirs = []
        for i in range(8):
            d = word(mem, DIR_TABLE + 2 * i)
            self.dirs.append(d - 0x10000 if d & 0x8000 else d)

    def addr(self, x, y):
        """$8436: row_table[y] + x, as an offset into buf."""
        return (word(self.mem, ROW_TABLE + 2 * y) + x - DECODE_BASE) & 0xFFFF

    def put(self, a, tile):
        if 0 <= a < len(self.buf):
            self.buf[a] = tile

    def line_from(self, a, count, direction, tile):
        """$8464: draw `count` cells (8-bit DEC/BMI loop), return end pointer."""
        c = count & 0xFF
        delta = self.dirs[direction & 7]
        while True:
            c = (c - 1) & 0xFF
            if c & 0x80:
                return a
            self.put(a, tile)
            a = (a + delta) & 0xFFFF

    def fill_rect(self, x, y, w, h, tile):
        """$8498: h rows of w cells."""
        a = self.addr(x, y)
        rows = h & 0xFF
        while True:
            rows = (rows - 1) & 0xFF
            if rows & 0x80:
                return
            col = w & 0xFF
            while True:
                col = (col - 1) & 0xFF
                if col & 0x80:
                    break
                self.put(a + col, tile)
            a += MAP_W

    def outline(self, x, y, w, h, tile):
        """$84D7: right w-1, down h-1, left w-1, up h-1."""
        a = self.addr(x, y)
        a = self.line_from(a, w - 1, 2, tile)
        a = self.line_from(a, h - 1, 4, tile)
        a = self.line_from(a, w - 1, 6, tile)
        self.line_from(a, h - 1, 0, tile)

    def build(self, rec, level):
        # $8226: seeds  ($3E = seed[level], $3F = 0)
        s2, s1 = rec[0x04 + level], 0
        objs, probs = rec[0x18:0x1C], rec[0x1C:0x20]
        # $8043: random fill, map rows 1..21, cols 0..39
        for row in range(1, MAP_H):
            for col in range(MAP_W):
                s1, s2 = next_random(s1, s2)
                tile = 0x01
                for i in range(4):
                    if s1 < probs[i]:
                        tile = objs[i]
                self.buf[(row + 2) * MAP_W + col] = tile
        # $85A7: steel border
        self.outline(0, 2, 40, 22, 0x07)
        # $8518: object list at $2420 ($FF-terminated, 8-bit index)
        y = 0x20
        while y < RECORD_LEN:
            code = rec[y]
            if code == 0xFF:
                break
            tile = code & 0x3F
            args = [rec[(y + k) & 0xFF] if y + k < RECORD_LEN else 0 for k in range(1, 6)]
            x0, y0, w, h, inner = args
            kind = code & 0xC0
            if kind == 0x00:                      # point, 3 bytes
                self.put(self.addr(x0, y0), tile)
                y += 3
            elif kind == 0x40:                    # line: len, dir, 5 bytes
                self.line_from(self.addr(x0, y0), w, h, tile)
                y += 5
            elif kind == 0x80:                    # filled box + inner, 6 bytes
                self.fill_rect(x0, y0, w, h, tile)
                self.fill_rect(x0 + 1, y0 + 1, w - 2, h - 2, inner)
                y += 6
            else:                                 # outline box, 5 bytes
                self.outline(x0, y0, w, h, tile)
                y += 5
        return [list(self.buf[(r + 2) * MAP_W:(r + 3) * MAP_W]) for r in range(MAP_H)]


def decode_cave(mem, n, level):
    rec = cave_record(mem, n)
    return rec, Decoder(mem).build(rec, level - 1)


def live_map(mem):
    return [list(mem[MAP_BASE + r * MAP_W:MAP_BASE + (r + 1) * MAP_W]) for r in range(MAP_H)]


# --- output ------------------------------------------------------------------
def render(grid, color=False, hexmode=False):
    lines = []
    for r, row in enumerate(grid):
        if hexmode:
            cells = " ".join("%02X" % t for t in row)
        elif color:
            cells = "".join("\x1b[%sm%s\x1b[0m" % (tile_info(t)[1], tile_info(t)[0]) for t in row)
        else:
            cells = "".join(tile_info(t)[0] for t in row)
        lines.append("%2d %s" % (r, cells))
    return "\n".join(lines)


def header(rec, level):
    lv = level - 1
    return ("%s  level %d  |  need %d diamonds  value %d (extra %d)  time %d  |  "
            "amoeba/magic time %d" % (cave_name(rec[0]), level, rec[0x09 + lv], rec[0x02],
                                      rec[0x03], rec[0x0E + lv], rec[0x01]))


def digits(mem, addr, n):
    return "".join(str(mem[addr + i]) for i in range(n))


def legend(grids):
    seen = sorted({t for g in grids for row in g for t in row})
    out = ["legend:"]
    for t in seen:
        ch, _, desc = tile_info(t)
        out.append("  %s  $%02X  %s" % (ch, t, desc))
    return "\n".join(out)


def main():
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__, formatter_class=argparse.RawDescriptionHelpFormatter)
    ap.add_argument("dump", help="64 KB RAM dump ($0000-$FFFF) of the running game")
    ap.add_argument("--cave", type=int, help="decode cave 1-20 (A-P = 1-16, intermissions 17-20)")
    ap.add_argument("--level", type=int, default=None, help="difficulty level 1-5 (default: level in dump, $5E)")
    ap.add_argument("--all", action="store_true", help="decode all 20 caves")
    ap.add_argument("--diff", action="store_true", help="compare decoded current cave with the live map")
    ap.add_argument("--color", action="store_true", help="ANSI colours")
    ap.add_argument("--hex", action="store_true", help="print tile IDs in hex")
    ap.add_argument("--legend", action="store_true", help="print the tile legend")
    a = ap.parse_args()

    mem = load_dump(a.dump)
    level = a.level if a.level else mem[0x5E] + 1
    if not 1 <= level <= 5:
        sys.exit("level must be 1-5")
    shown = []

    if a.all or a.cave:
        caves = range(1, CAVE_COUNT + 1) if a.all else [a.cave]
        for n in caves:
            if not 1 <= n <= CAVE_COUNT:
                sys.exit("cave must be 1-20")
            rec, grid = decode_cave(mem, n, level)
            print(header(rec, level))
            print(render(grid, a.color, a.hex))
            print()
            shown.append(grid)
    else:
        n = mem[0x5D]
        grid = live_map(mem)
        print("LIVE  %s  level %d  |  time %s  diamonds %s/%s  value %s  |  cave in $2400: %s"
              % (cave_name(n), mem[0x5E] + 1, digits(mem, 0xAB, 3), digits(mem, 0xB0, 2),
                 digits(mem, 0xB2, 2), digits(mem, 0x51, 3), cave_name(mem[0x2400])))
        print(render(grid, a.color, a.hex))
        shown.append(grid)
        if a.diff and 1 <= n <= CAVE_COUNT:
            _, dec = decode_cave(mem, n, mem[0x5E] + 1)
            print("\nDECODED (cave start state)")
            print(render(dec, a.color, a.hex))
            same = sum(1 for r in range(MAP_H) for c in range(MAP_W) if dec[r][c] == grid[r][c])
            print("\n%d / %d cells identical to the live map (%.1f%%)"
                  % (same, MAP_W * MAP_H, 100.0 * same / (MAP_W * MAP_H)))
            shown.append(dec)

    if a.legend:
        print(legend(shown))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
